# Mechanisms and measures

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How this chapter's sources were read

This chapter is written from two hundred and sixty-eight claim records, each
read against the lines of its source and then checked by a reviewer who had not
written it. That review amended over half of them. Not one of the amendments was an arithmetic error. They
were hedges that had hardened into assertions, scopes widened past the source, a
direction reversed, percentages whose denominator belonged to a different set,
and notes that misdescribed the paper they annotated. Several of this chapter's
sources are abstract-only in this project's corpus, which bounds what can be
claimed from them, and the text says so wherever it matters.
:::

One gene, one protein was always an approximation. It stopped being a useful
one as soon as transcripts could be counted directly. The harder question that
replaced it is which of a gene's several transcripts matter, and why.

Three processes generate those transcripts: exons spliced in different
combinations, transcription starting in different places, and polyadenylation
ending the molecule in different places. Each of the three affects at least half
of human protein-coding genes [@carrion2023alternativetranscripts]. So isoform
is not a synonym for splice variant, and this book keeps the two terms apart.

This chapter is the one the rest of the book points back to. It sets out the
machine that performs splicing, the signals it reads, the vocabulary used to
name the outcomes. Then come the measurements used to quantify them, and the
bounds on each. The bounds are the part worth reading twice. Almost every
headline figure in this field is a function of a threshold, a denominator or a
counting rule. The sections below give the rule alongside the number wherever a
source states one.

## The machine that removes an intron {#sec-mechanism}

The machine is not an enzyme: five small nuclear ribonucleoproteins, U1, U2,
U4, U5 and U6, work with hundreds of further proteins. The assembly is built
fresh on every pre-mRNA through an ordered series of intermediates named E, A,
B and C. Only the first of those forms without ATP
[@borao2021earlyspliceosome].

The two ends of an intron are recognised by different machinery and in a
definite order. U1 engages the 5' splice site, while SF1 and the U2AF
heterodimer together recognise the 3' splice site; U2 arrives later, by
displacing SF1 [@borao2021earlyspliceosome].

What gets written as a single 3' splice site is three separate elements working
together. The branchpoint, the polypyrimidine tract and the terminal AG
dinucleotide are distinct, so recognition can fail without the AG itself being
touched [@borao2021earlyspliceosome].

Two of the three are weaker than their names suggest. The branchpoint supplies
the acceptor nucleotide for the first chemical step. In humans its sequence is
barely a consensus: YUNAY, with one position unconstrained, against a
near-invariant UACUAAC in budding yeast [@borao2021earlyspliceosome]. The
polypyrimidine tract has an operational definition rather than a motif. It is
an uninterrupted run of pyrimidines between the branchpoint and the terminal
AG, its strength counted in uridines, and U2AF65 binds it there
[@borao2021earlyspliceosome].

The 5' side is no better defined. Only the first two bases, GU, are reliably
conserved, and every other position varies. The last three nucleotides of the
upstream exon also contribute to how tightly U1 binds. Degeneracy plus that
exonic extension gives a broad range of interaction strengths rather than a match
or a mismatch [@borao2021earlyspliceosome].

That degeneracy is the point rather than a defect. One argument holds that
splice site motifs degenerated over evolution specifically to permit regulated
splicing. On the same argument, the accompanying rise in spliceosome complexity
underlies the shift from mainly constitutive splicing in budding yeast to
regulated and alternative splicing in humans [@borao2021earlyspliceosome]. On
that reading constitutive and alternative splicing are two regimes of one
mechanism, not two mechanisms.

### The chemistry is two reactions and one intermediate

The intermediate was characterised before the machine was. In a cell-free
reaction on an adenovirus transcript, the intermediate proved branched rather
than linear. The 5' end of the intron is joined to a single adenosine near the
3' splice site by a 2'-5' bond. That adenosine keeps its ordinary 3'-5' bond to
the next nucleotide. The excised intron retains the branch and ends in a
guanosine with a free 3' hydroxyl. The phosphate at the new exon-exon junction
comes from the precursor's 3' splice site [@padgett1984intermediates].

What performs the chemistry is RNA, and the materials were yeast extracts
depleted of U6 and reconstituted with synthetic U6 bearing single sulfur
substitutions at twenty positions in both diastereomers. On those materials,
metal rescue shows that U6 catalyses both reactions. It does so by positioning
the divalent metals that stabilise the leaving group at each step
[@fica2013rnacatalyzes]. The reaction is two phosphotransesterifications run by
a two-metal mechanism proposed earlier, one metal holding the attacking
nucleophile and the other the leaving group [@fica2013rnacatalyzes]. The
evidence establishes a catalytic role for RNA rather than ruling one out for
protein. The distinction matters for a dispute taken up below.

The metals are held by RNA tertiary structure. Genetics, crosslinking and
biochemistry in yeast show base triples within U6, analogous to those in group II
intron domain V, promoting both metal binding and both chemical steps. Because
one element of those triples is the sequence that defines the 5' splice site, the
same structure that organises the metals also brings the substrate alongside them
[@fica2014triplex].

A structure caught immediately after branching shows that the machine does not
release what it has cut. At 3.8 angstroms, on spliceosomes assembled in yeast
extract, the cleaved 5' splice site stays close to the catalytic magnesium site
in the U2/U6 triplex. The freed 5' exon is held between two Prp8 domains and
base-paired to loop 1 of U5. The intron downstream of the branch runs out
towards the Prp16 helicase [@galej2016branching].

Whether Prp8 itself contributes to catalysis is disputed. A crystal structure
showed that its RNase H-like domain can bind a metal in crystallo. It also
showed that mutations compromising that binding impair exon ligation, which the
metal-rescue authors note raises the possibility of a catalytic role. Those
same authors state that they found no evidence of a catalytic interaction
mediated directly by a metal between the 3' splice site and that site. They
suggest instead that Prp8 may primarily promote formation of the RNA catalytic
core without being part of it [@fica2013rnacatalyzes].

### The cycle runs on ATPases, and not all of them unwind

Activation was assigned to a named enzyme and a named substrate early. Adding
hydrolysable ATP to an immunopurified native complex containing U1, U2, U5 and
duplex U4/U6 particles disrupts the U4/U6 base pairing and releases free U4 and
U6. A mutation in the helicase-like domain of Brr2 prevents it. It happens with
no pre-mRNA added, which led those authors to propose a U4/U6 cycle uncoupled
from splicing [@raghunathan1998brr2].

The 5' splice site changes partners through a helicase working as a clamp.
Cryo-electron microscopy of the human pre-B complex at 3.3 angstroms, and of
the human tri-snRNP at 2.9, is the evidence. It shows U1 inserting the helix it
forms with the 5' splice site between the two RecA domains of the Prp28
DEAD-box helicase. ATP-dependent closure of those domains releases the site to
pair instead with the U6 ACAGAGA box, presented as a mobile loop. Those authors
propose that this then triggers Brr2 to relocate to its loading sequence in U4
[@charenton2019splicesitetransfer].

An ATPase in this machine need not unwind anything. Chemical structure probing
of purified yeast complexes before and after Prp2 acts shows double-stranded
RNA staying wound. The two reactants of the first step gain flexibility. Those
authors describe Prp2 as acting principally on the ribonucleoprotein rather
than on a duplex [@bao2017prp2].

Catalytic activation in human spliceosomes is two ATP-dependent stages rather
than one. Inactivating Aquarius stalls a complex halfway through activation.
Its structure shows PRP2 translocating along the intron while it strips the RES
complex away, opens the SF3B1 clamp and unfastens the branch helix.
Translocation stops six nucleotides downstream of the branch site. Aquarius
then enables the dissociation of PRP2 together with the SF3A and SF3B
complexes, which those authors say promotes relocation of the branch duplex for
catalysis [@schmitzova2023activation].

### The minor spliceosome {#sec-minor}

A second, parallel machine exists, and it is tiny by comparison. The minor
U12-dependent spliceosome excises about 0.5 per cent of introns. Roughly 700
human genes carry a U12-type intron, against 19 genes in *Drosophila*. The
typical minor-intron-containing gene holds exactly one of them among many major
introns [@akinyi2021minorspliceosome]. A review of the same subject puts the
share below 0.4 per cent and names the particles as U11, U12, U4atac, U5 and
U6atac [@elmarabti2021minorintron]. The two figures come from two reviews
rather than from two counts, and nothing read here reconciles them.

The two intron classes are told apart by their signals rather than their
chemistry. A polypyrimidine tract is a feature of major introns only. The minor
3' splice site is recognised by ZRSR2 instead of the U2AF heterodimer. Because
U12 signals are far better conserved, they support correspondingly less
alternative splicing [@akinyi2021minorspliceosome]. Better signals, less
regulation, which is the degeneracy argument above running in reverse.

## Fidelity is enforced by ATPases, and it competes with catalysis {#sec-proofreading}

Proofreading is not a separate department from splicing. The metal-rescue work
above reports that proofreading and discard mechanisms, competing with
catalysis at both steps, had held back the application of metal rescue to this
reaction. The same work reports that the direct effectors of catalysis were
identified only after ATP-dependent proofreading was eliminated. Those authors
did that to enhance the potential for rescue [@fica2013rnacatalyzes]. The
fidelity machinery had to be switched off before the chemistry could be
measured.

Changing an ATPase's activity changes which substrates the spliceosome accepts.
Alanine and ATPase-motif mutants of yeast Prp5p alter which branch region is
accepted. Improved splicing of a suboptimal intron in cells tracks with reduced
ATPase activity across a series of motif III mutants. Compensatory U2 changes
that increase branch region pairing abrogate the effect. That links a fidelity
event to a defined physical structure [@xu2007branchfidelity].

Lowering activity at a second ATPase lets a mutant branch site be used. Seven
alleles of yeast PRP16 all map to the region shared by RNA-dependent ATPases.
They allow an intron whose branch site is mutated to be spliced at the mutant
cytosine. Three of the mutant proteins were purified and each showed reduced
ATPase activity. Steady-state levels of intermediates and products are reported
as evidence for a route that discards incorrectly branched substrates. Those
authors separately propose that slower hydrolysis gives an aberrantly formed
lariat intermediate more time to take the productive branch instead
[@burgess1993discardpathway].

Rejection is reversible, which is why a discard route has to exist. The assay
was an in-vitro one, sensitised to proofreading by disrupting a metal-ligand
interaction at the catalytic centre. In that assay, inactivated spliceosomes
cleaved the 5' splice site when Prp16 was disabled, at a reduced rate. Prp16
associates with spliceosomes before that cleavage although it does not promote
splicing of a genuine substrate until afterwards. The discard pathway that
reversible rejection requires was shown to need the ATPase Prp43. Those authors
conclude that fidelity at 5' splice site cleavage and at exon ligation share a
common ATP-dependent framework [@koodathingal2010proofreading].

The prototype proofreader turns out to have two roles rather than one. In yeast
whole-cell extracts, Prp16 was found to promote rather than prevent the use of
aberrant 5' splice sites and mutated branchpoints. It is not required for
branching on wild-type pre-mRNA. It facilitates the reaction independently of
ATP when a 5' splice site is mutated or Cwc24 is absent. And it still prevents
the use of nearby cryptic branch sites. Those authors attribute this to Prp16
stabilising or destabilising interactions through the step-one factor Cwc25.
They conclude that it can either enhance or impede the use of faulty splice
sites. On their account it has dual roles in choosing the 5' splice site and
the branch site, exercised through both ATP-dependent and ATP-independent
activity [@chung2023prp16].

Proofreading at the second step may be a stability sensor rather than a motor.
Purified spliceosome iCLIP on complexes stalled at defined stages shows Prp16
bound along the whole single-stranded stretch between the branchpoint and the
3' splice site. Prp22 binds diffusely downstream of the branchpoint before exon
ligation, then narrowly in the downstream exon afterwards. Those authors read
that as arguing against processive translocation. Depleting the exon-ligation
factor Prp18 destabilises Prp22 binding to the pre-mRNA
[@strittmatter2021psiclip].

An equivalent control operates in human cells and has an identified activator.
Rapid depletion of DHX15, followed by analysis of nascent and mature RNA, shows
that suboptimal introns are repressed by it. The suboptimal ones are those with
weak splice sites, those with multiple branch points, and those that are
cryptic. SUGP1 is a G-patch factor that activates this function, in a way
dependent on both DHX15 ATPase activity and the SUGP1 ULM domain
[@feng2023dhx15].
## The five event names, and the patterns they miss {#sec-event-classes}

Five names carry most of the field's vocabulary: exon skipping, mutually
exclusive exons, intron retention, alternative donor and alternative acceptor;
they were inherited rather than derived. The paper that formalised event
nomenclature says so, then points out that real annotations hold many patterns
none of the five describes [@sammeth2008nomenclature].

How many is measurable: splicing patterns too complex for any of the five names
run from 23.18 per cent of all events in one reference annotation to 35.4 per
cent in another. So roughly a quarter to a third of annotated alternative
splicing has no textbook label [@sammeth2008nomenclature].

The four simple classes do hold a stable rank order across three human
annotations. The order runs exon skipping first, then alternative donor, then
alternative acceptor, with intron retention last. That denominator is stated
rather than implied. It counts events with a simple splicing pattern, involving
at most two alternative splice sites, and not correlated with a variable
transcription start or polyadenylation site [@sammeth2008nomenclature].

The spectrum is not the same inside and outside the reading frame. In coding
sequence, exon skipping accounts for 50.9 per cent of local events against 37.9
per cent in 5' untranslated regions. Intron retention runs the other way, 2.1
per cent in coding sequence against 8.4 per cent in 5' untranslated regions.
Those authors read that as selection against in-frame stop codons
[@sammeth2008nomenclature]. Retained introns reach about 12 per cent of all
events in transcripts with no annotated reading frame, on an annotation worth
naming. That annotation is a 2007 freeze built by mapping expressed sequences
onto pilot regions rather than the whole genome. It holds 2,247 noncoding
against 1,332 coding transcripts [@sammeth2008nomenclature].

Mutually exclusive exons are rare, at 12 to 14.5 per cent of the complex event
pool depending on the annotation, and well behind the skipping of two
consecutive exons. That share is taken against the complex pool rather than the
simple-event denominator above, so it does not place the class in the rank order
of the other four. Those authors attribute the scarcity to the
more elaborate mechanism mutual exclusivity requires
[@sammeth2008nomenclature].

### The same five classes have three different names

Three vocabularies are in use for one set of distinctions. The nomenclature paper
writes alternative donor and alternative acceptor [@sammeth2008nomenclature]. The
paper that introduced percent spliced-in writes alternative 5' splice site and
alternative 3' splice site [@wang2008alternative]. A 2017 genome-wide study
writes differential exon inclusion, glossed as exon skipping, alongside
alternative 5' and 3' exon splicing [@hatje2017mutuallyexclusive]. A reader
meeting all three will not know they are reading about the same events.

That second vocabulary also already named three classes the five traditional
names cannot express. Tandem untranslated regions, where a pair of
polyadenylation sites in one terminal exon gives a shorter or longer 3'
untranslated region. Mutually exclusive 3' untranslated regions, where the same
choice instead yields two distinct terminal exons. And mutually exclusive 5'
exons, where alternative promoter use gives messages with distinct 5'
untranslated regions [@wang2008alternative].

One pair of terms is worth a warning. A single source states in passing that the
literature uses cassette exon as another name for a skipped exon
[@huang2013ganoderma]. That is an assertion of interchangeable usage, not a
definition of either term and not a reason to prefer one. This book treats them
as synonyms on its own authority, and the glossary says so.

### One number across two decisions

A percent spliced-in value sits across two separate splicing acts. An
intron-centric reformulation splits it into a 5' and a 3' index, one per intron
end. Those authors describe that as deconvoluting the reaction into its two
elementary acts [@pervouchine2013introncentric]. Where the two indices
disagree, a single value hides the disagreement.

Event-level inclusion also carries a laboratory signature. Values inferred from
isoform abundances by one estimator varied substantially between laboratories
even among nineteen judged high quality. A principal component analysis of
event-level inclusion grouped the data by laboratory rather than by biological
sample [@wang2026benchmarking].

## An exon's position is not a property of the exon {#sec-exon-type}

The categories first, internal and last are not disjoint, and how many exons
are hybrid is set by a threshold. The input was 353,677 annotated meta-exons in
one human cell line, half discarded as unexpressed. On that input, a
junction-read imbalance cutoff of 0.3 classified about 60,000 exons as
internal, about 16,000 as terminal and about 30,000 as hybrid. Hybrid
first-internal and hybrid internal-last exons were each about 13 per cent of
expressed exons. A conservative criterion added from a probabilistic model left
3.8 per cent of exons hybrid [@fiszbein2022hybridexons]. Those figures are the
paper's own and they do not reconcile with one another. The three classes do not
sum to the expressed set, the two hybrid subtypes at 13 per cent each come to
more than the count given for all hybrids, and the 3.8 per cent counts all
hybrids rather than one subtype. Checking any of that is arithmetic this book is
doing rather than a published reconciliation. What the set of numbers does
establish is that the count is a function of the cutoff.

Those authors name the gap in the taxonomy directly, calling it the unsolved
exon type problem. How to classify exons uniquely as first, internal and last
has not been solved. A hybrid exon will be called internal by RNA-seq and
terminal by an assay anchored on transcript ends. Even so, both readings are
correct for different molecules in the same cell type
[@fiszbein2022hybridexons].

Position also changes between tissues on a large scale, and that paper states
the size of the effect two ways. Its abstract reports more than 100,000 exons
switching between internal and terminal use across the tissues analysed. Its
results text gives more than 130,000 and puts that at about 10 per cent of all
exons analysed [@fiszbein2022hybridexons]. The two figures are both the paper's
own. The denominator behind that 10 per cent is not stated as the meta-exon set
quoted above, and 130,000 at 10 per cent would imply a far larger one.

Inside a composite terminal exon a splice site and a poly(A) site compete in
the same sequence. Tipping the balance toward splicing produces a spliced
truncated transcript. Overexpressing the spliceosomal factor TRAP150 forced use
of a cryptic 3' splice site and yielded spliced prematurely polyadenylated
transcripts. That activity was seen in composite but not in authentic terminal
exons, and was strengthened by weakening U1 or by interfering with elongation
or termination [@lee2014trap150].

## Intron retention is not a class like the others {#sec-intron-retention}

One event class differs in kind rather than only in frequency. A molecule
carrying a retained intron still holds a splice-site pair the spliceosome could
in principle use. So the observed state is not necessarily a finished one.
Those authors also argue that the earliest steps of spliceosome assembly
suffice by themselves to hold such an RNA in the nucleus
[@jacob2017intronretention].

So an unspliced intron in polyadenylated RNA does not establish that a splicing
decision was made. It is compatible with a finished message, with an intermediate
accumulating ahead of a slow rate-limiting step, or with a transcript
deliberately stalled awaiting a later decision [@jacob2017intronretention]. Every
other event name describes a choice that has been made. This one describes a
state that may still be pending.

The standard measure is percent intron retention, the share of a gene's
transcripts keeping a given intron. It is computed from reads crossing the two
exon-intron junctions against those plus the reads crossing the exon-exon
junction made by removing it. There is a further requirement, that reads
accumulate evenly at both junctions and in the intron's middle. On that
measure, the material was polyadenylated RNA from about forty human and mouse
cell and tissue types. In it, about 77 per cent of multiexonic genes carry at
least one intron retained at 10 per cent or more in at least one type. And 35
per cent carry one retained at 50 per cent or more
[@braunschweig2014intronretention]. The headline prevalence is a function of
where the threshold sits.

Those authors argue retention works by lowering expression. It acts broadly to
reduce transcripts present at relatively low abundance that often have no
physiological relevance in the cell or tissue where they are detected. Those
authors call that tuning the transcriptome [@braunschweig2014intronretention].

### The measurement is contested, and the tools were adopted before any benchmark

A second survey from the same period says the first was not looking at the same
thing. The detained-intron authors allow that the two sets may partially
overlap. They then state that the introns the other survey enriched in
polyadenylated transcripts sat preferentially in untranslated regions. On their
account those introns also ran opposite to gene expression and were often
degraded by nonsense-mediated decay. They conclude that many of them are a
different population from detained introns, which are nuclear and not decay
substrates [@boutz2015detainedintrons], and the other survey never answers.

Detention is not a single mechanism either. Three assays of the
precursor-product relationship put the MAT2A detained-intron transcript down as
a dead-end molecule degraded in the nucleus rather than a store later spliced
into message. That is the role the field had established for the CLK1 detained
intron. Cotranscriptional splicing of the MAT2A introns rose when cells were
deprived of S-adenosylmethionine [@pendleton2018mat2a]. One detained intron is
a dead end and another is a reservoir.

The tools came before the benchmark: reviewers who catalogued the available
intron-retention software in 2019 recorded that none of it had been
systematically benchmarked at that date. So the tools the field had already
adopted were in use before any systematic benchmark of them existed
[@monteuuis2019intronretention]. That review makes no statement about ad hoc or
pairwise comparisons.

What produces a false retained intron is specific and named. The causes are
genomic DNA carried through into the library and unprocessed precursor counted
as mature message. A third is intronic stretches whose coverage is unreliable
because they are repetitive or poorly mappable. That review relays the list
from an earlier review it cites rather than measuring any of them
[@monteuuis2019intronretention].

The authors of a replacement metric state that the estimators then in use
suffer from biases and artefacts severe enough to impair the analysis of
retention. They report that their own stabilised ratio agreed better with
retention computed from long reads of the same cell line. On their account it
was also more consistent between technical replicates [@broseus2020sirfinder].

The benchmark, when it came, was severe. Retained introns called from short
reads were compared against a reference set called persistent in long reads
from the same biological specimens. The comparison used a persistence threshold
those authors define. The eight short-read tools were in strong disagreement
with one another, at a Fleiss kappa of 0.113. In the same comparison, 47.7 per
cent of all retention calls made by any tool were not reproduced by a second
tool [@david2022retainedintrons]. Those authors draw the conclusion plainly:
the tools detect retention with both poor recall and poor precision. Because of
that, they hold the completeness and the validity of a large share of the
retained introns reported by commonly used methods to be in question. No tool
they tested reached an F1 score above 0.26 [@david2022retainedintrons].

That is the strongest negative result in this chapter, and it bears on every
retention figure quoted anywhere in this book.

## Microexons {#sec-microexons}

A size class can be missed by a whole field for a methodological reason.
Microexons were largely left out of earlier analyses of splicing in cancer
because exons that short require computational approaches built for them
[@head2021srrm4].

The class has no agreed boundary: one source defines microexons as exons of 3
to 15 nucleotides [@irimia2014neuronalprogram]. A second gives 30 nucleotides
or fewer and treats them as a subset of cassette exons rather than an event
class of their own [@parada2021microexonator]. A third takes 3 to 27
nucleotides from two earlier papers it cites [@parada2026microexoncode]. Three
published cut-offs, and a count that depends on which is used.

What singled the class out was not its size. Those authors set out what they
called the largest programme of coordinated neural-regulated alternative
splicing then described in mammals. Inside that programme, microexons showed
both the most striking evolutionary conservation and the most nearly
switch-like regulation of any event type [@irimia2014neuronalprogram]. Most
annotated microexons keep the reading frame. The characterised examples work by
modulating protein-protein interactions needed for the development and function
of the nervous system, a property relayed from two reviews
[@parada2026microexoncode].

They have a single dominant regulator: most neural microexons are controlled by
the neuron-specific factor nSR100, also called SRRM4. That factor binds
enhancer motifs in the intron immediately adjacent to the microexon rather than
within it [@irimia2014neuronalprogram]. Its expression is largely confined to
neural tissues [@head2021srrm4].

The reason they were invisible is mechanical. On simulated reads a
general-purpose spliced aligner lost sensitivity sharply below 10 nucleotides
of exon and two others below 8. Run with default settings the three produced
false discovery rates of 0.43, 0.33 and 0.13. The last of those is
indistinguishable from the 0.12 and 0.10 of two pipelines written for the
purpose [@parada2021microexonator]. The problem was the aligner, not the
biology.

A purpose-built pipeline over 289 datasets from eighteen mouse tissues across
nine embryonic and postnatal stages returned 2,984 microexons. Of those, 37 per
cent were absent from the reference transcript models. Of the 326 whose
inclusion changed during neuronal development, 18 per cent were absent from a
dedicated splicing database [@parada2021microexonator].

The catalogue was still incomplete in 2026. The candidate set was roughly two
million sites, defined as intronic stretches of 3 to 27 nucleotides flanked by
sequences resembling splice sites. Against that set, an analysis of 4,790 bulk
human samples and 47,380 single nuclei from human cortex detected 1,514
microexons absent from both the reference transcript models and the dedicated
splicing database. Of those, 292 were spliced
differently between neural and non-neural material. A further 1,115 new
microexons were found in mouse, 95 of them neurally spliced
[@parada2026microexoncode].

How an exon this short is defined at all now has a mechanistic answer. Nascent
RNA sequencing in neuronal cells showed microexon splicing to be not merely
cotranscriptional but faster than transcription of the surrounding gene. The
intron upstream of a microexon is removed before the downstream intron has
finished being synthesised. Those authors argue that this leaves the
microexon's non-canonical downstream donor site as the only remaining option
[@gordon2026microexondefinition].

## Mutually exclusive exons {#sec-mutually-exclusive}

The rarest of the five classes was also the worst served by annotation. A human
annotation of the period held only 158 mutually exclusive exons in 79
protein-coding genes. The criteria those authors state are genomic adjacency,
compatible splice sites, and never appearing together in one protein isoform
[@hatje2017mutuallyexclusive].

Deep sequencing changed the number in both directions. The input was 515
samples, comprising over fifteen billion reads from 31 tissues and organs,
twelve cell lines and seven developmental stages. Reading them raised the count
from 158 to 1,399 supported by at least one junction read per exon, and 855
supported by at least three. The same pass showed that 29 of the 158 already
annotated as mutually exclusive are not spliced that way at all
[@hatje2017mutuallyexclusive]. The spread between 855 and 1,399 is a threshold,
not a discovery curve.

Genes can carry more than one cluster, and in one case the clusters are nested.
Against 554 genes holding a single cluster, four genes each hold three and
three each hold four. In one of those, a cluster of four variant exons sits
inside a pair of exon sets that are themselves mutually exclusive
[@hatje2017mutuallyexclusive]. One human gene carries a cluster of ten mutually
exclusive exons. That cluster is absent from mouse and rat, having been lost in
their common ancestor [@hatje2017mutuallyexclusive]. The extreme form of the
class in human is missing from the rodents usually used to study splicing.

What enforces the exclusivity is mostly unexplained. Across 629 validated human
clusters, five, 0.79 per cent, have splice sites of incompatible spliceosome
types. Fifty-seven, 9 per cent, are cases of potential steric interference. In
those, a donor site and a branch point are too close together for the
intervening intron to be removed. And 377, 60 per cent, contain exons whose
lengths are not divisible by three, so including two would break the frame. Yet
reads joining two exons were found for only 83 of those 377, 22 per cent
[@hatje2017mutuallyexclusive]. That leaves 484 clusters held apart by something
else. Those authors name RNA-protein interactions, snRNP and splicing-factor
interactions and competing RNA secondary structure as proposals they cite to
others. They note on the same line that such competing structures are usually
not conserved across long evolutionary distances [@hatje2017mutuallyexclusive].

A decay pathway does part of the enforcement in at least one animal. In
*Caenorhabditis elegans*, where those authors state they characterised the
whole repertoire, 29 clusters were confirmed in 27 genes. Twenty-two consisted
of homologous exons and five had intervening introns too short to be excised,
which accounts for 27 of the 29 and is not given as a partition.
The fidelity of the choice in fourteen relied at least in part on
nonsense-mediated decay [@kuroyanagi2014mutuallyexclusive]. That connection is
taken up in @sec-as-nmd.
## Most isoform differences sit at the transcript ends {#sec-ends}

Three distinct processes generate transcript isoforms: alternative exon splicing,
alternative start-site choice and alternative polyadenylation. Each touches at
least half of human protein-coding genes, which is why isoform cannot be treated
as a synonym for splice variant [@carrion2023alternativetranscripts].

The weighting between them has been estimated several times, and splicing is
the minority explanation. Across 23 human cell types, alternative splicing
explains tissue-dependent isoform differences for at most 35 per cent of genes.
In the same types, 53 per cent of the tissue-dependent exonic regions showed no
or only weak evidence of ever being spliced out [@reyes2018altstart]. A
promoter-level survey of developing and adult cerebellum reaches the same
conclusion by another route. It reports 61,525 distinct messages from 29,589
promoters for 15,669 protein-coding and 7,624 noncoding genes. Those authors
conclude that transcript variants are predominantly generated by alternative
transcription rather than alternative splicing [@pal2011cerebellar]. That
abstract names no species for the cerebella and no other study on the line to
agree with.

The share of splicing variation that could plausibly change a protein is
smaller still. Only about 15 per cent of tissue-dependent splicing involves
exons belonging to principal isoforms, and the rest is concentrated in
untranslated exons and in non-coding or minor transcripts [@reyes2018altstart].

Where coding sequence does vary between isoforms, the variation sits at the
ends. Coding exons in the variable 5' and 3' ends produced by alternative
initiation and termination carry about four times more alternative nucleotides
than the core coding region. That region can only be diversified by splicing
[@shabalina2014proteinends].

### The dominant process depends on where you count, and on how you count

The cleanest decomposition is also the one needing the most care. The set was
74,955 expressed human genes defined from combined short- and long-read
evidence. Of those, 65,193 genes, 87.0 per cent, sat away from the vertices of
a start-site, end-site and splicing simplex. Start-site choice dominated 4,844,
6.5 per cent, end-site choice another 4,906, 6.5 per cent, and splicing only 12
genes, 0.02 per cent [@saberi2026transcriptomearchitecture].

Those numbers need three qualifications, and the same authors supply the
material for all three. The decomposition is a formula rather than a
measurement. It counts, per gene, the distinct start sites, distinct end sites
and distinct exon chains. It then converts splicing into the ratio of twice the
exon-chain count to the sum of the start- and end-site counts, and normalises
the three to sum to one. A gene's position is therefore a function of all three
counts and of the rules by which each was defined upstream
[@saberi2026transcriptomearchitecture]. The 87 per cent is a residual, not a
category: it is what is left after three vertices are defined. A gene with one
isoform lands at the exact centre of the simplex. And dominant has no
operational definition in that source. The 0.02 per cent for splicing is a
statement about where genes sit in a constructed coordinate system, not a
measurement of how much splicing does.

A different decomposition, on mammalian transcripts sorted by domain, says the
answer depends on which part of the transcript is counted. Splicing was the
dominant source of variation inside the coding sequence, and alternative
initiation dominated in 5' untranslated regions. Alternative termination
dominated in 3' untranslated regions [@shabalina2010connections]. That analysis
states its attribution rule and reports it as robust. Alternative nucleotides
in a first exon lying between the most upstream and most downstream start site
were charged to initiation. Those in the last exon between the extreme
termination sites were charged to termination, and everything left over to
splicing. Site separations were accepted between 100 and 500,000 nucleotides, a
relaxed range those authors say gave results similar to a stringent one
[@shabalina2010connections].

So the question which process matters most has no answer independent of a
counting rule. The three published attempts assign the weight differently and
each states its own rule.

### Start sites

Having more than one promoter is ordinary rather than exceptional, and the
alternatives are separately regulated. A tagging survey reports differentially
regulated alternative start sites as a common feature of protein-coding genes,
commonly placing a different amino terminus on the protein
[@carninci2006genomewide].

In annotation the class is large: in one release, 12,767 of 26,304 genes
carried more than one message. Of the multi-isoform genes, 7,708, or 60 per
cent, had alternative promoters. In 43 per cent of those the first exons did
not overlap at all, leaving 3,296 genes with isoforms whose first exons are
wholly distinct [@jacox2010altpromoters]. Each of those percentages has a
different denominator, which is why the counts are given alongside them.

Mammalian promoters fall into two architectural classes with different
initiation behaviour: conserved, TATA-box-enriched promoters starting
transcription at one well-defined position. The other class is more plastic,
broad, evolvable CpG-rich promoters. The paper stating the division sequenced
tags corresponding to several hundred thousand start sites in mouse and human
[@carninci2006genomewide]. The difference reflects two different machines
rather than two amounts of one. In fly cells, the promoters of developmentally
regulated genes had DNA that readily associated with the canonical polymerase
II pre-initiation complex. Housekeeping promoters did not, recruiting other
factors instead. Tethering those factors to a promoter was by itself enough to
produce the dispersed pattern [@serebreni2023promoterclasses].

The familiar two-way split rests on thresholds chosen by hand. Clustering the
same start-site distributions systematically with a non-parametric
dissimilarity measure instead produced a third class. In that class essentially
every start maps to one genomic position, distinct from sharp promoters where
the position varies by a few nucleotides [@zhao2011tssclustering]. That third
class is likely to be an artefact of measurement rather than biology. Those
promoters lacked the epigenetic marks of messenger RNA promoters, and a
substantial subset mapped upstream of ribosomal protein pseudogenes. Those
authors say at least some are likely due to mapping errors. They attribute
those errors to the similarity of ribosomal gene promoters combined with a
known guanosine-addition bias in the libraries [@zhao2011tssclustering].

What a measurement calls one promoter is often several starts merged. A survey
across primary cells, cell lines and tissues reports that many promoters are
composite entities made of several closely separated start sites. The
expression profiles of those sites across cell types are independent of one
another [@promoterlevel2014expressionatlas]. The merging rules are explicit
where they are stated. One widely reused set of human peaks was called by
decomposition-based peak identification over 988 libraries, then filtered to a
robust subset. Robust means peaks containing a start site with more than 10
reads in at least one sample and one tag per million [@varshney2019isletatlas].

A gene can also acquire a promoter by acquiring an exon. Blocking the splicing
of an internal exon reduced transcription from promoters near it. Creating a
new spliced exon switched on transcription from previously cryptic promoters.
Those authors name that phenomenon exon-mediated activation of transcription
starts, and report it for thousands of genes
[@fiszbein2019transcriptionstarts]. The causal arrow runs from splicing to
initiation.

### Polyadenylation

Choosing among a gene's several poly(A) sites yields transcripts differing in
3' untranslated region, in terminal exon, or in coding potential. None of those
is a splicing difference [@huang2026apacancer].

The term covers two consequences that should not be pooled. Tandem choice within
the last exon leaves the protein untouched and changes only the regulatory
elements carried. Sites used upstream, in introns, internal exons or alternative
terminal exons, can truncate the protein outright [@huang2026apacancer].

Two hexamers, AAUAAA and AUUAAA, account for about 75 per cent of
polyadenylation signals while every other hexamer is used at under 3 per cent.
Measured dissociation constants were generally inversely correlated with
frequency. The low-frequency hexamers AAGAAA and AACAAA nevertheless supported
good cleavage [@huang2025lowfrequencypas]. The hexamer is a poor predictor on
its own. The input was more than 8,700 human 3' untranslated sequences and
157,775 polyadenylated expressed sequence tags. Against that input, about 5,600
tag-supported ends were found, and a known signal was present at only 73 per
cent of them. Ten single-base variants of AAUAAA occurred often enough to be
significant, potentially representing 14.9 per cent of real signals
[@beaudoing2000signalusage]. That source does not add the two figures together,
and neither should a reader.

How many sites a gene has is contested, and the published counts are not
independent attempts at one quantity. An expressed-sequence-tag survey found
28.6 per cent of the messages examined, not of the genes, carrying two or more
sites. In that survey, sites closer to the coding sequence tended to carry
variant hexamers, and the most 3' site the canonical one
[@beaudoing2000signalusage]. A method built to avoid oligo-dT priming artefacts
found about 79 per cent of mouse messenger RNA genes and about 66 per cent of
long noncoding RNA genes with alternative polyadenylation [@hoque2012analysis].
Those are different denominators in different species by different methods.

Three published human site counts differ by a factor approaching two, and two
of the three come from one project. One atlas reports 569,005 clusters from 221
samples and twelve protocols on one genome build. A second reports 290,168 from
107 samples and one protocol on an older build. The third, 392,912 from 78
samples and nine protocols on that older build, is the first atlas's own
earlier release. The citing paper describes itself as an update of that release
[@herrmann2019polyasite].

A site in an atlas is a cluster, not a position, and the merging is explicit.
Raw 3' ends were sorted by read support and each absorbed into a stronger site
within 12 nucleotides on either side. Clusters carrying an annotated signal
were then merged if the combined width stayed within 25 nucleotides. Clusters
with no annotated signal were merged whenever they lay within 25 nucleotides of
each other [@herrmann2019polyasite]. The thresholds are acknowledged to be
arbitrary. A survey of these pipelines reports that internal priming is removed
by heuristic filters, such as six consecutive adenines in ten nucleotides or
fifteen in twenty. The same survey reports that no unified standard exists. It
also reports that adjacent cleavage sites are grouped with only slight
differences in distance, 25 nucleotides in two pipelines and 24 in a third.
Those authors call the strategy subjective and arbitrary, and liable to produce
clusters spanning several real sites. On their account it understates the
diversity of polyadenylation profiles between species and especially in plants
[@ye2026polyaseqtrap].

Whether the scatter of ends around a site is biology or noise is itself
disputed. The prevailing reading is that clustering reflects imprecise cleavage
near one site. The elongation-rate authors argue against it: imprecise cleavage
is a property of the processing complex acting on RNA, and so is independent of
the polymerase. On their account that cannot explain why the relative levels of
isoforms inside a cluster move with polymerase speed
[@geisberg2022elongationlinkage].

### The machinery, and what sets the choice

Recognition of the hexamer had already been assigned to a four-subunit core
before the structural work. A complex of CPSF160, WDR33, CPSF30 and Fip1 was
sufficient for AAUAAA recognition. The interactions underpinning its assembly
and its mechanism of recognition were not understood. That paper's own result
is the architecture of the core. Quantitative binding assays identify a lysine-
and arginine-rich motif at the amino terminus of WDR33, alongside the zinc
fingers of CPSF30, as a critical determinant of specificity
[@clerici2017cpsfassembly].

The cut is made by one subunit acting as a nuclease. Purified recombinant
CPSF-73 had RNA endonuclease activity, and mutations disrupting zinc binding in
its active site abolished it. The structure placed the two-zinc active site at
the interface of a metallo-beta-lactamase domain and a beta-CASP domain
[@mandel2006cpsf73endonuclease]. Isolated CPSF does not cut: specific and
efficient endonuclease activity was reconstituted from purified human proteins
only when the seven-subunit complex was combined with cleavage stimulatory
factor, cleavage factor IIm and the multidomain protein RBBP6
[@boreikaite2022rbbp6].

The downstream element is read by a separate complex. Human cleavage
stimulatory factor carries two copies each of CStF77, CStF64 and CStF50. The
RNA-recognition motifs of CStF64 bind G- and U-rich sequence downstream of the
cleavage site. Cleavage factor IIm is a heterodimer of Pcf11 and Clp1
[@boreikaite2023endprocessing].

The standard account of why one site is chosen is a race between the machinery
and the polymerase. In the kinetic model as reviewed, a higher cellular
concentration of CPSF and its accessory factors promotes use of the proximal
sites that emerge first and are often suboptimal. In the same model, lower
concentrations enforce use of the distal, canonical ones
[@boreikaite2023endprocessing].

Core factors do not all pull the same way. Knocking each down in mouse
myoblasts and sequencing 3' ends showed Pcf11 and Fip1 enhancing use of
proximal sites. CFIm25, CFIm68, PABPN1 and PABPC1 promoted distal ones. Strong
cis-element biases were reported for the sites regulated by CFIm25 and CFIm68,
or by Fip1, rather than for all six factors. The distance between competing
sites played an important part [@li2015apacode].

One factor's effect has been measured directly. Of 12,273 transcripts whose
terminal exon was covered more than thirtyfold, 1,453 shifted their 3' end
reproducibly after CFIm25 was knocked down. Of those 1,453, 1,450 shifted
toward the proximal site [@masamha2014cfim25].

Polymerase speed sets where the cut falls. That slowly elongating mutant
polymerases shift the whole profile of ends upstream and fast ones shift it
downstream is those same authors' earlier publication, cited here as previously
shown. What this paper adds is that the shift is continuous from one isoform to
the next at nucleotide distances within a cluster of sites. It barely crosses
from one cluster to the next. That holds in yeast and, for the slow mutant, in
human cells [@geisberg2022elongationlinkage].

### Polyadenylation inside an intron

A cryptic site inside an intron is actively suppressed rather than merely weak.
Functional knockdown of U1 with an antisense morpholino caused premature
cleavage and polyadenylation at cryptic signals in numerous precursors. Those
signals sat frequently in introns within 5 kilobases of the transcript start.
It did not happen when splicing was blocked at U2 instead, by morpholino or by
spliceostatin A, unless the U1 morpholino was also present
[@kaida2010u1telescripting].

The splicing machinery holds these sites down under normal conditions rather
than only when perturbed. Knocking down the U1 protein U1-70K or the U2 protein
SF3b155, or blocking U1 with an oligonucleotide, substantially changed which
sites upstream of the last exon were used. Every splicing-factor knockdown
raised those isoforms overall. Knocking down the U2 auxiliary factor U2AF65
changed far fewer [@li2015apacode].

The class is large: of the mouse messenger RNA genes with alternative
polyadenylation, 53 per cent had a site in an intron or an upstream exon
[@hoque2012analysis].

Intronic sites split into two annotated shapes plus a third that neither
explains. The definition of an intronic site here is a cluster more than 200
base pairs from the nearest annotated splice site. On that definition, a strict
set yielded 2,846 skipped terminal exons, 2,251 composite terminal exons, and
1,482 clusters where polyadenylation coexisted with canonical splicing. Those
authors name that third class spliced polyadenylated introns, and find it in
about 13 per cent of genes expressing more than one intronic site
[@vlasenok2023intronicpa].

That third class is partly a measurement artefact, and its authors say so. They
estimate conservatively that spliced polyadenylated introns, which carry a
poly(A) tail but are released as part of the lariat, make up almost a quarter
of all intronic polyadenylation events. Two thirds of them are already present
in a published atlas. Those authors conclude that 3' end sequencing may
therefore overestimate the rate of intronic polyadenylation
[@vlasenok2023intronicpa].

In the fly, whether a signal is used depends on whether it sits in an intron.
Reporter and genomic assays found signals used when they lay in exonic
sequence, but not when the same signals lay in an intron. Deletion of the 5'
splice site restored their function. A whole-transcriptome analysis found
intronic signals used very rarely [@tikhonov2013competitionwithinintrons].

### End choice and splicing are not independent

The two are coupled, and the coupling has been measured. In one mammalian
transcript-domain analysis the number of alternative nucleotides attributed to
alternative initiation correlated positively with the number attributed to
splicing within 5' untranslated regions. The correlation was 0.19 in one
transcript set and 0.21 in the other [@shabalina2010connections].

The promoter a transcript comes from changes how it is spliced. Swapping
promoters in front of an otherwise identical fibronectin minigene changed how
much of one exon was included. The effect tracked promoter structure rather
than promoter strength. Those authors present that as the first evidence that
alternative splicing is coupled to promoter-specific transcription
[@cramer1997promoterstructure].

The route from promoter to splice site runs through elongation speed. Inserting
the SV40 enhancer into the same minigene suppressed inclusion of that exon. The
minimal enhancer of two 72-base-pair repeats was sufficient. Deleting one of
the two repeats raised inclusion and restored responsiveness to an SR protein.
The accompanying drop in elongation showed up both as a higher ratio of short
proximal to full-length transcripts and as higher polymerase density upstream
of the alternative exon [@kadener2002enhancerelongation]. That mechanism is
taken up in @sec-kinetic.
## The signals in the sequence {#sec-cis}

Splice site strength became a number by modelling a site as a distribution
rather than as a consensus. A maximum entropy framework approximates a short
motif's distribution with the maximum entropy distribution consistent with
low-order marginal constraints. That admits dependencies between non-adjacent
as well as adjacent positions. Against decoys, the best of those models
discriminated human donor and acceptor sites better than previous probabilistic
models [@yeo2004splicingsignals].

What a strong site buys is limited, and there is a named class of
counterexamples. Pseudoexons are intronic sequences flanked by strong splice
sites that are not included in messages. They show nucleosome depletion rather
than the nucleosome occupancy found over real exons
[@tilgner2009exonrecognition].

The score also failed to separate fast introns from slow ones. 15,671 human
introns common to six cell lines were split into quartiles by mean nascent
splicing index. Consensus scores, polypyrimidine tract lengths and
branchpoint-to-3'-splice-site distances showed no differences between
quartiles. Intron length did, with first-quartile introns roughly twice the
median length of fourth-quartile introns, 2,118 against 1,077 base pairs
[@bedi2021cotranscriptional].

What weak means is partly counterintuitive: hyperstabilising the duplex between
U1 and the 5' splice site in human cells and extracts did not decrease splicing
efficiency. Instead it increased site recognition and exon inclusion. Low
complementarity significantly increased exon skipping and RNA degradation.
Those authors note the first result is unlike what had been observed in budding
yeast [@freund2005u1duplex].

Cis elements and splice sites also substitute for one another as a function of
intron length. Among human introns shorter than 1.5 kilobases, exonic enhancer
density rises with intron length at R = 0.159 for constitutive introns. That
falls to R = 0.086 once exon-end base composition is corrected for. Above that
length, enhancer density stops tracking intron length and splice-site strength
rises instead [@dewey2006compensatorysignals].

### The regulatory elements were found by screen and by prediction

Enhancers were found by prediction and then confirmed. A statistical analysis
of exon, intron and splice-site composition nominated ten enhancer motifs.
Representatives of all ten raised splicing in cells. Point mutants of those
sequences showed sharply reduced activity [@fairbrother2002rescuepredictive].

Silencers were found the other way round. A screen of a random decanucleotide
library in a splicing reporter recovered 141 silencer decamers, of which 133
were distinct. Most could be clustered into seven putative motifs, some
resembling the sequences bound by hnRNP H and hnRNP A1
[@wang2004systematicidentification].

Intronic elements followed the same functional-selection logic. A fluorescence
screen of random 15-nucleotide inserts beside an alternative exon in a minigene
recovered 125 distinct active intronic sequences from 226 sequenced isolates.
Of 18 tested individually, 16 silenced the exon and two enhanced it
[@culler2010intronicelements].

An element's identity as enhancer or silencer is not a property of the sequence
alone. Of 16 intronic sequences selected as silencers in one cell line, 12 kept
the same direction of effect in a second. Four acted as enhancers there in the
same reporter. Those authors suggest differences between the lines in
trans-acting factor levels, in total RNA levels or in rate of decay. Their own
conclusion from that line is that most of the selected sequences retain
function in a second cell line [@culler2010intronicelements].

The cis contribution has also been probed by brute force. Splicing was read out
for over two million synthetic minigenes carrying more than 100 million bases
of degenerate sequence. The great majority of hexamer motifs measurably shifted
splice-site choice when placed inside an alternative exon. The effects of
several motifs added together rather than combining cooperatively
[@rosenberg2015determinants].

Whether the sequence is available at all depends on structure. Exonic segments
immediately upstream of a 5' splice site are more base-paired in retained
introns than in spliced ones of the mouse embryonic stem cell transcriptome.
Forcing those loops into stems impaired splicing of two reporters. The worst
defect came when all four loops upstream of one 5' splice site were hybridised
[@saha2018exonicstemloops].

### Position, not composition {#sec-position}

Splicing regulation is positional rather than merely compositional. The authors
of an RNA map derived for the neuron-specific factor Nova report that where its
sequence clusters sit in a precursor determines the outcome. They also report
that the map predicted correctly whether Nova would inhibit or enhance
inclusion of a given exon [@ule2006novaprediction].

The rule has a physical reading: Nova bound to an exonic cluster changed the
complexes assembled on the precursor and blocked U1 binding along with
inclusion. Nova bound to an intronic cluster enhanced spliceosome assembly and
inclusion [@ule2006novaprediction].

The same shape is reported for whole protein families. SR proteins enhance
splicing only when recruited to the exon, and interfere when the same site is
relocated to the intronic side of the regulated 5' splice site
[@erkelenz2013commonmechanisms]. hnRNP proteins are reported to show the same
pair of opposing activities with the position dependence reversed. So on this
model the antagonism between the families follows from where each binds, rather
than from an intrinsic difference between enhancer and silencer proteins
[@erkelenz2013commonmechanisms].

Activation and repression act on different steps. An activating factor of
either family makes a splice site easier to recognise at the very first stage,
when the exon is being defined. A repressing one instead builds non-productive
complexes that arrest assembly before the two sites are paired
[@erkelenz2013commonmechanisms].

Tethering splits the rule into protein parts. For RBFOX1 and RBFOX2 the
C-terminal domain alone was sufficient to activate an exon when tethered to the
downstream intron. Repression from the upstream intron required both that
domain and the central RNA-recognition motif [@sun2012tetheredmechanisms].

Positional rules are now read off two data types at once. Two hundred and three
pairings of enhanced CLIP with knockdown sequencing in the same cell line
covered 139 RNA-binding proteins across two lines. They yielded a wide variety
of averaged binding-density maps around knockdown-responsive events
[@vannostrand2020rbpmap]. The classical division of labour survives that
genome-scale test in direction. SR protein binding was typically associated
with exons that lost inclusion when that protein was knocked down. hnRNP
binding was typically associated with exons that gained it
[@vannostrand2020rbpmap].

### Five bounds on the positional rule

The rule is real and it is weaker than it looks, in five separate ways.

Shared position does not imply shared outcome. Two closely related factors show
overlapping positional enrichment at the exons included on knockdown of one.
Yet across the exons responding to knockdown of both, the splicing changes
caused by knocking down each correlate at only R-squared 0.03
[@vannostrand2020rbpmap].

Binding where the rule predicts an effect need not produce one. Of 87 cassette
exons carrying nearby cross-links for one factor yet showing no significant
change in the knockdown data, 13 were retested. Only four of those retested
changed detectably. That retest is reported on the same line as data not shown
[@jangi2014rbfox2autoregulation].

The underlying signal is sparse, and across one large collection of
crosslinking datasets, the mean share of a factor's called peaks falling
anywhere inside a knockdown-altered cassette exon region is under 1 per cent.
It rises only to 1.3 per cent for known splicing regulators and 1.9 per cent
for spliceosome components. Those authors give that as what limits the power of
the peak-based approach, while saying that maps built on read density remain
highly useful [@yee2019rbpmaps].

And the background can set the conclusion. The same signal for one SR protein at
knockdown-excluded exons is higher than at any of the four cassette-exon classes
but equivalent to constitutive exons. A constitutive-exon background would
suggest the factor is unchanged there, while a native cassette-exon background
shows it enriched [@yee2019rbpmaps]. The difference is enrichment against
equivalence, not a reversal of direction, and it still changes what the map
appears to say.

Position dependence need not operate inside the exon either. In synthetic
designer exons carrying no natural regulatory sequence, a single enhancer
raised inclusion three- to fourfold at each of six evenly spaced positions.
There was no significant difference between positions, except three differences
of 5 per cent or less in the chromosomal constructs [@arias2015designerexons].

### The two protein families, and where the antagonism stops

The antagonism was established as a dose effect. In vitro, an excess of SF2/ASF
promoted inclusion of an appropriate alternative exon, while an excess of hnRNP
A1 caused its skipping. From that those authors propose that the ratio of the
two proteins may in some cases regulate alternative splicing
[@mayeda1993exonskipping].

The same experiments showed where the model stops. Excess hnRNP A1 did not
cause skipping of every alternative exon. Those authors give as examples of
what it depended on how large the internal alternative exon was and how strong
the preceding intron's pyrimidine-rich tract was. They call the effect not
universal rather than closing the list [@mayeda1993exonskipping].

It is not only a property of in vitro reactions. Transient overexpression of
SF2/ASF in cells shifted cotransfected reporters towards proximal 5' splice
sites, drove a neuron-specific exon to be included and stopped an abnormal
skipping event. Overexpression of hnRNP A1 shifted the same reporters towards
distal sites [@caceres1994overexpression].

Both families have a modular build whose parts are functionally separable. SR
proteins carry one or two RNA-recognition motifs and a carboxy-terminal
arginine and serine repeat. Deleting the second motif of SF2/ASF left a protein
still active in alternative splicing, but with altered specificity in 5' splice
site selection [@caceres1997modulardomains]. For hnRNP A1, conserved
phenylalanines in each of its two motifs were needed to modulate alternative
splicing but not for general precursor binding. The carboxy-terminal
glycine-rich domain was needed for splicing activity, for stable binding and
for optimal RNA annealing [@mayeda1994conserveddomains].

Phosphorylation sits above the antagonism as a control layer. On one SR
protein, two kinases divide the serines of its arginine-serine domain between
them by residue context, rather than each taking one end of the domain. One
acts on arginine-serine repeats and the other additionally on serine-proline
dipeptides [@aubol2013clksrpk].

An exon's inclusion is normally set by several factors at once. The inputs were
splicing-sensitive microarrays, crosslinking data and cDNA sequencing for hnRNP
proteins in human cells. On those inputs, more than half of all alternative
splicing events detected were regulated by more than one hnRNP protein. Some
combinations were synergistic and others antagonistic
[@huelga2012cooperativeregulation].

Factors do not hold their own levels independently either. In mouse embryonic
stem cells one factor alters decay-coupled splicing events in other RNA-binding
proteins. For one of those, the negative autoregulation of its own transcript
was not significant at steady state. It appeared only when that protein was
overexpressed and the first factor knocked down. Those authors propose that one
factor sets the threshold at which another autoregulates
[@jangi2014rbfox2autoregulation].

A large part of that cross-regulation is invisible unless decay is blocked.
Among curated cassette exons in RNA-binding-protein transcripts with nearby
cross-links for one factor, 45 would generate a premature termination codon on
inclusion and 20 on skipping. Half of the factor-dependent changes among the
six such genes assayed could not be seen without inhibiting nonsense-mediated
decay. Those six genes were picked because their decay-coupled events had
changed by 0 to 5 per cent on knockdown under standard conditions
[@jangi2014rbfox2autoregulation]. Standard conditions hide the effect, which is
why @sec-as-nmd matters for regulation and not only for decay.

### The splicing code as a prediction problem {#sec-code}

One splicing code treated a splicing decision as prediction. It drew on
hundreds of features of the RNA, taken in combination, to forecast how
thousands of exons shift inclusion from one tissue to another. Its authors
reported regulatory strategies including unexpectedly large feature
combinations, and features sitting deeper inside introns than had been
appreciated [@barash2010deciphering].

A code predicts the extremes better than the middle. A deep network was
evaluated by five-fold cross-validation on exons drawn from 11,019 mouse
alternative exons, each described by 1,393 features. A ten-junction-read
threshold had removed 45.8 per cent of the training examples. On that input the
network reached an area under the curve of 89.3 for the low-inclusion class and
88.3 for the high-inclusion class in brain, but 79.4 for the medium class
[@leung2014deepsplicingcode].

The accuracy reported is partly an accuracy on its own dataset. Tested against
data from a different experiment, the same network showed about a 1 to 4 per
cent decrease in area under the curve for brain across all exons. On the subset
defined as tissue-variable, the decrease was about 4 to 5 per cent.
Tissue-variable means a change in inclusion of at least 0.15 for one tissue
pair [@leung2014deepsplicingcode].

The predictors are not merely memorising natural genomes, which a synthetic
test settles. Eleven predictors were scored on thousands of heavily recoded
synthetic variants whose splicing was measured per position by long-read
sequencing. On that test, the modern deep-learning predictors kept strong
performance and the ranking stayed largely stable. The tools ignoring
long-range sequence context fell behind chiefly by scoring unspliced positions
highly [@bellidomolias2026splicingpredictors].

### The share of an exon that is splicing information is disputed

The field's two ways of asking this have not agreed. Conservation-based
genome-wide studies put functional enhancer content at a few per cent of coding
sequence. Mutagenesis of model exons returned figures from about a fifth of the
sequence to nearly all of it. The authors reporting that spread argue their own
estimate sits at the lower experimental end [@savisaar2018exonicselection].

Their estimate is that about 15 to 20 per cent of fourfold degenerate sites are
part of a functional exonic splicing enhancer. The denominator is a filtered
set of 10,879 human protein-coding genes compared with macaque, and most of
them are under strong rather than weak constraint
[@savisaar2018exonicselection].

The size of that estimate turns on how many motifs are counted, and one widely
quoted smaller figure is conditional. In the same gene set, a single
conservative enhancer motif set puts about 18 per cent of coding nucleotides
inside a motif. The unconditional measurement is that about a quarter to a
third of the fourfold degenerate positions in those motifs are functional. The
smaller figure of 4 to 6 per cent of all fourfold degenerate sites follows only
on one condition. That condition is that the authors' failure to control for
contextual mutation biases is taken to have overestimated the functional
fraction by about a third [@savisaar2018exonicselection]. Quoting 4 to 6 per
cent without that condition states a conclusion the source makes conditional.
Both 15 to 20 per cent and 4 to 6 per cent are shares of fourfold degenerate
sites rather than of all exonic positions, so they are two estimates of one
quantity under two motif sets rather than two different quantities.

Predicted enhancers do behave like sequences under selection in living
populations. The denominator was about 121,000 annotated internal human exons,
a database those authors confined to exons with no cDNA evidence of alternative
splicing. Across those exons, polymorphisms disrupted a predicted enhancer
hexamer in 10.9 per cent of cases, against 13.6 per cent for mutations
simulated in the same exons under pseudogene-derived substitution frequencies.
That is a relative risk of 0.80 on the pooled data [@fairbrother2004verify].

Whether splicing enhancers show positive as well as purifying selection is
disputed, and both sides are worth stating. Of the enhancer motif sets tested
in the 10,879-gene set, only one showed evidence of positive selection, while
the three others and their combined set showed none. The figures are 15 to 25
per cent of fourfold degenerate motif sites under selection, and 18.6 per cent
for the combined set [@savisaar2018exonicselection]. Those authors present this
as contradicting an earlier report of positive selection on two motif classes.
They add in the next sentence that the earlier work analysed constitutively and
alternatively spliced exons separately and found positive selection only in the
former. On their account, pooling the two could hide it
[@savisaar2018exonicselection]. That is the authors' own reconciliation, not a
reader's, and the earlier analysis stands on its own terms. Calibrated on
intronic substitution rates, it reported a strong avoidance of synonymous
changes disrupting a predicted enhancer or creating a predicted silencer. In
constitutive exons it reported an excess of changes creating enhancers and
destroying silencers, which those authors read as positive selection for
splicing-promoting mutations [@ke2008compensatory].
## The decision is made on the nascent transcript {#sec-kinetic}

### The spliceosome may recognise the exon first

The unit first recognised may be the exon rather than the intron. Precursors
built with elongated second exons lacking a 5' splice site were deficient in
spliceosome assembly and splicing in vitro. The same substrates assembled and
spliced normally once a 5' splice site was placed at the end of that exon,
provided the exon was under 300 nucleotides long. U2 was required to protect
that site. Those authors read this as direct communication during early
assembly between the factors binding the two sites flanking one exon
[@robberson1990splicesites].

Exon size and intron size are not independent constraints. Internally expanded
exons placed in vertebrate genes were skipped when the flanking introns were
large, and included when the same large exons were flanked by small introns.
Both exon and intron size became problematic at approximately 500 nucleotides.
Those authors add that the size at which recognition failed was itself
influenced by exon and intron sequence, so the figure is not a fixed threshold.
They note that large introns and small exons are the vertebrate rule while the
opposite holds in lower eukaryotes [@sterner1996splitgenes].

The switch between the two recognition modes was later measured and given a
length. Splicing assays show that recognition across the intron stops once
introns reach 200 to 250 nucleotides, and that beyond that size sites are
recognised across the exon instead. The same assays show that recognition
across the intron is significantly more efficient. So an exon with weak splice
sites is included more when the flanking introns are short
[@foxwalsh2005splicesitepairing].

The mode in force can be read off alternative splice site usage. In one
database of alternative site usage, pairing goes preferentially to the sites
lying nearest one another across the intron when the competing sites sit within
short introns. It goes to the sites nearest one another across the exon when
the competing sites sit within large flanking introns. So the spliceosome pairs
whichever sites are closest within the unit it is using
[@carranza2022proximity].

A timing measurement in a fly embryo cuts against the length rule. Native
elongating transcript sequencing in early embryos found heterogeneous dynamics.
Some RNAs were spliced immediately after the intron was transcribed, and others
showed no splicing across the first 100 nucleotides of the downstream exon.
Although the proportion of spliced reads was related to intron size, introns of
every size showed intron definition [@prudencio2022drosophila]. That is a
different species and a different assay from the in-vitro threshold, and the
two have not been reconciled.

There is now a proposed physical route by which exon definition could happen on
the polymerase. One polymerase subunit is reported to interact directly with
U2AF1, the factor binding the 3' AG dinucleotide, to initiate 3' splice site
recognition. On that report, those initial exon-definition events are in turn
what let U2AF2 be recruited into a heterodimer with U2AF1. On the same report,
that recruitment also triggers the release of U2AF1 from the elongating
polymerase. That gives two phases, in which polymerase-assisted site
recognition precedes polymerase-independent assembly [@shao2025cycling].

### Co-transcriptional does not mean immediate

Splicing happens on the nascent transcript, and one group reads its data as
placing it at a distance from the transcription machinery rather than at it.
Nanopore sequencing of nascent RNA in human and fly cells found that
co-transcriptional splicing occurs only after the polymerase has transcribed
several kilobases of precursor. The same work found that inhibiting the
branch-site recognition complex abolished co-transcriptional splicing in both
species. It also found that splicing order does not strictly follow the order
of transcription, with neighbouring human introns tending to be spliced
concurrently [@drexler2020nanocop].

The fraction has been measured with an explicit time window. Splicing was
assessed for about 17,000 introns expressed across six human cell lines, one
non-cancer and five cancer. Of the introns interrogated, fewer than half had
been spliced within thirty minutes of their synthesis. Efficiencies differed
between cell lines and within genes, and first introns were the least
efficiently spliced of all [@bedi2021cotranscriptional].

A fission yeast is different, and long-read sequencing of nascent multi-intron
transcripts found most of them fully spliced, consistent with rapid
co-transcriptional splicing. The same work found an unexpectedly high
proportion either fully spliced or fully unspliced. Those authors read that as
splicing of any one intron depending on the splicing status of the others. A
temperature-sensitive mutation in the homologue of vertebrate U2AF65 increased
the fully unspliced fraction [@herzel2018nascent].

### Elongation rate, and why the window model is not enough

Changing how fast the polymerase moves changes which exon is chosen. Expressing
in human cells a human equivalent of a fly point mutation in the largest
polymerase subunit, which confers a lower elongation rate, altered alternative
splicing of one fibronectin exon and of an adenovirus precursor. Resplicing of
a Hox gene was stimulated in fly embryos mutant for the same change. Those
authors offer this as direct proof of elongation control of alternative
splicing in cells [@delamata2003altsplicing].

Slowing the polymerase does not reliably increase inclusion. Taking one CFTR
exon as a model, skipping can also follow from slowed elongation. Slowed
elongation promotes recruitment of a negative factor onto the UG repeat at that
exon's 3' splice site, displacing U2AF65 from the overlapping polypyrimidine
tract. Weakening the exon's 5' splice site increased that factor's binding and
the skipping, while strengthening its usage had the opposite effect. Those
authors state that in most cases slow elongation instead allows weak splice
sites to be recognised and raises inclusion [@dujardin2014exonskipping].

The sharpest result against the simple model is that fast and slow usually
agree. The cell lines were isogenic, expressing a resistant polymerase large
subunit carrying either a fast or a slow substitution. In those lines, 198 of
the 319 exons with enhanced inclusion in the fast mutant were also more
included in the slow mutant. And 332 of the 636 exons skipped in the fast
mutant were also skipped in the slow one. So the slow and fast mutants usually
did not have opposite effects on a given exon. Those authors say a simple
window-of-opportunity model does not easily account for that
[@fong2014optimalrate]. An optimal rate explains that pattern; a monotonic one
does not.

### Chromatin, and which way the arrow points

Nucleosomes sit over exons, and the pattern may not require transcription at
all. Stable nucleosome occupancy was found within human and worm exons and was
stronger in exons with weak splice sites. Nucleosomes sat centrally within
exons rather than proximal to the splice sites. The ratio of occupancy within
an exon to that upstream of it correlated with inclusion level. The same exonic
patterns were present in genes that were not expressed
[@tilgner2009exonrecognition].

Whether the histone mark or the nucleosome is the signal is contested. Analysis
of nucleosome positioning in humans, flies and worms found higher occupancy
over exons than introns. Those authors link that to differential GC content and
to nucleosome-disfavouring elements. Four modifications were found enriched in
exons. Even so, those authors state that the previously described enrichment of
H3K36me3 in exons reflects the more fundamental phenomenon of increased
nucleosome occupancy along exons [@schwartz2009exonintron].

Marks can nonetheless change a decision rather than merely accompany one.
Distinctive signatures were found correlating with splicing outcome across a
set of human genes. Modulating those modifications caused splice site
switching. The marks acted by influencing the recruitment of splicing
regulators through a chromatin-binding protein. Those authors describe that as
an adaptor system by which the splicing machinery reads histone marks
[@luco2010altsplicing].

A local perturbation settles the direction for one locus. Histone-modifying
enzymes were fused to targeting domains and transfected into cells to alter
chromatin only locally. On that design, the targeted alternative exon was
included more when H3K9 di- and trimethylation rose locally, and was skipped
when a demethylase removed those marks. H3K9me3 was found on internal exons
genome-wide, and targeting the demethylase to a weak constitutive exon reduced
that exon's co-transcriptional splicing [@bieberstein2016tale].

The traffic also runs the other way. Intron-containing genes carry more
H3K36me3 than intronless genes in human cell lines and mouse primary T cells.
Inhibiting splicing impairs recruitment of the H3K36 methyltransferase and
reduces the mark, while activating splicing has the opposite effect. The
increase correlates with the length of the first intron. Yet the same line
reports that in intron-containing genes the mark's level is also proportional
