to transcriptional activity [@dealmeida2011setd2recruitment]. That last clause
is the confound: a mark that tracks transcriptional activity cannot be read as
a splicing signal without separating the two.

### Two decisions in one gene may or may not be independent

The question was put to a microarray measurement in 2007. Earlier
expressed-sequence studies had already found individual coordinated exon pairs,
and what those authors claim as new is the tissue-dependence and the extent.
Roughly 500 of the 3,044 mouse genes on that array carried between two and five
alternative exons. Every pairwise combination with sufficient signal in 20 or
more of the 27 tissues was tested for correlation. The comparator was the
average over 1,000 random samples of exon pairs drawn from different genes.
Those authors concluded that pairs of alternative exons in the same gene can be
regulated in a coordinated manner across mouse tissues
[@fagnani2007coordination].

A long-read comparison put a differently designed version of the question and
found no such dependence. Sequencing full-length transcripts from human and
macaque cerebellum, those authors report that the alternative processing events
along a transcript combine largely independently of one another. They treated
that independence as the reason thousands of real isoform combinations are
missing from annotation [@zhang2017primateisoforms]. That is a failure to
detect dependence in the combinations observed along single molecules, not a
measurement of correlation across tissues. The two designs can disagree without
either being wrong, and this book keeps both.

A third measurement finds coupling between kinds of event rather than between
exons. Genes carrying a hybrid first-internal exon were 1.3-fold more likely
than expected to carry a hybrid internal-last exon as well. The genes carrying
both were enriched for spliceosome components and splicing factors
[@fiszbein2022hybridexons].
## PSI: how much an exon is used {#sec-psi}

Percent spliced-in was introduced as the fraction of a gene's messages that
contain a given exon, estimated from read densities rather than raw counts. The
estimate is the density of inclusion reads divided by the sum of the inclusion
and exclusion densities [@wang2008alternative].

The quantity it estimates is not observable. What is observed is a count of
reads crossing each junction. One tool models that as a binomial draw whose
success probability is the inclusion fraction. So the reported index is an
inferred parameter of a model rather than a ratio of counts
[@vaquerogarcia2023majiq].

A point estimate alone also hides how much was behind it. A probabilistic
treatment of isoform ratios reported an estimate together with a statement of
confidence in it. It treated the fragment length distribution of paired-end
libraries as part of the model rather than as a nuisance [@katz2010miso]. The
same index value from a handful of reads and from several hundred is the same
number and not the same measurement.

Read depth is why the estimator needs a prior. One group adopts a Bayesian
estimator explicitly to improve the estimate where coverage over the junction
is low. Its prior encodes the empirical observation that most inclusion
fractions sit near zero or near one rather than in the middle
[@vaquerogarcia2023majiq].

The noise is a function of expression. Measured between biological replicates
of one condition, where the true change is zero, the spread of the index was
larger at low transcript abundance. So the same numerical change does not mean
the same thing at different expression levels [@trincado2018suppa2].

Separating the two reasons an index moves takes two variance components. A
hierarchical model built for the purpose keeps the sampling uncertainty of each
replicate apart from the variability between replicates. Those authors report
that pooling RNA or merging reads across replicates does not substitute for
replication, and is sensitive to outliers [@shen2014replicate].

The criticism of the simplest form is specific. An index computed as a
two-by-two table of inclusion against exclusion counts and tested with an exact
test has no term for biological variation. The authors making that criticism
point out that the data originally used to demonstrate the approach contained a
single sample per tissue. They add that its probabilistic successor still
compared one knockdown sample with one control [@anders2012dexseq].

An index need not be computed from reads at the event at all. One widely used
tool derives it arithmetically from transcript-level abundance estimates for
the isoforms that carry and skip the feature. That makes the index inherit
every assumption of the quantifier and of the annotation it ran against
[@trincado2018suppa2]. That is worth knowing before two papers' values are
compared.

How accurate the index is has been measured against two comparators, and the
answer depends on which. The three tools with relatively higher agreement
against a long-read reference built from the same reference materials reached
mean correlations of 0.41, 0.41 and 0.38. Against RT-qPCR instead, the same
three reached 0.62, 0.60 and 0.76. Coverage mattered throughout, with accuracy
and repeatability both poorer wherever coverage was low. Inclusion level told
as well, most of all in the middle of its range [@wang2026benchmarking].

## Expression and usage test different nulls {#sec-dtu}

Three questions are easy to conflate and are set out as three study designs.
Differential gene expression asks whether a gene's total transcriptional output
changed. Differential transcript usage asks whether the composition of its
isoform abundance spectrum changed. Differential transcript expression asks
whether an individual transcript changed. They are different null hypotheses, not
different resolutions of one [@soneson2016differential].

![A two-isoform gene under the three nulls. Total output up or flat on one axis,
isoform proportions shifted or flat on the other, with each cell labelled by
which test fires. Only gene-level testing is blind to the bottom-left
case.](../figures/dge-dtu-dte.svg){#fig-dge-dtu-dte width=100%}

The distinction can be separated by construction, and a simulation that does so
makes it concrete. Of 15,017 genes with expressed transcripts, 70 per cent were
left unchanged. Ten per cent had every isoform shifted by the same fold change,
so output changed while proportions did not. Ten per cent had a single isoform
shifted, which changed proportions only where the gene had another isoform
expressed. The remaining 10 per cent had the abundances of two isoforms swapped,
changing proportions with no change in output at all [@love2018swimming].

Built as a generalised linear model, a usage test separates two terms that
would otherwise be confounded. One is for the overall fold change of the gene.
The other is for the effect of condition on the fraction of the gene's reads
falling in a given counting bin. Only the second is the usage parameter
[@anders2012dexseq].

A usage test is also not a set of per-transcript tests. The null one tool
rejects is that the whole vector of isoform proportions within a gene is the
same in both conditions. An overdispersion term is added to the multinomial, so
that replicates are allowed to differ from one another for biological and
technical reasons [@nowicka2016drimseq].

The two-stage framework controls an error rate defined across both stages.
Genes are screened first, and only the transcripts of the genes that pass are
then tested. That means a gene can be called as having changed its isoform
composition while no individual transcript within it survives the confirmation
stage [@love2018swimming]. A reader who expects a named transcript from every
called gene will be disappointed by design.

Exon-level and transcript-level usage answer the same gene-level question but
not the same transcript-level one. Both can report that a gene's splicing
changed, while only transcript usage names which isoforms were used more and
which less. Exon-level counting additionally suffers from exons whose
boundaries differ between isoforms [@baldoni2025dtu].

Proportions are also not quite what they look like. The proportion a quantifier
reports is the probability that a read came from a transcript, which depends on
that transcript's length. Those authors argue the quantity a usage test should
compare is the probability that the gene expresses the transcript, which does not
[@tiberi2020bandits].

### Dominance is a convention

Dominant isoform is two claims collapsed into one phrase, and one paper
separates them. The major transcript is whichever has the highest expression
within a gene. A dominant transcript is a major transcript expressed at
considerably more than any minor one. Operationalised as the major transcript
being at least twice as abundant as the next, that held for almost 80 per cent
of expressed genes in primary tissues [@gonzalezporta2013dominanttranscript].

Isoform fraction is used as an operational quantity: the ratio of a given
isoform's abundance to the total expression of its gene. Its differential form
is the arithmetic difference between that ratio in the two conditions compared
[@rai2026isoformswitching].

Where a usage change is called a switch of the dominant isoform, the threshold
is a convention rather than a measurement. One study classified a gene as a
major switch when the largest absolute change in any isoform's fraction reached
0.15, and a partial redistribution at 0.08. That placed 91 of 174 genes with
significant usage change in females, and 181 of 339 in males, in the major
class [@naidu2026transcriptswitching]; moving the threshold moves the count.

## A transcript quantifier fits a model rather than counting reads {#sec-quantification}

A transcript quantifier does not count reads. It fits a generative model of how
reads would have been produced from a set of transcripts and finds the
abundances making the observed reads most likely. That is because counting only
the reads that map to one transcript discards data, and gives wrong answers
exactly at the alternatively spliced genes [@li2011rsem].

The model says that, absent bias, the chance of drawing a fragment from a
transcript is proportional to the number of copies of that transcript
multiplied by its effective length. That is why abundance and length cannot be
separated from a read count without the length model [@patro2017salmon].
Effective length is the mean number of positions inside a transcript at which a
fragment of the library's observed size distribution could have started. So a
transcript shorter than the typical fragment has a much smaller effective
length than its nominal length [@li2011rsem].

The output is generally not an integer. A read often fits more than one
transcript of its gene, and so cannot be assigned to one. Because of that, the
reported count is the expected number of fragments assigned to that isoform
under the fitted model [@li2011rsem]. No read is double counted and none is
thrown away.

Such a quantifier can report how uncertain it is. Sampling from the posterior
of the same model yields a posterior mean and a credibility interval per
transcript, built to cover two sources of doubt at once. Those are the
randomness of sampling reads and the ambiguity of assigning them [@li2011rsem].

How well those intervals work depends on the annotation supplied. Intervals
estimated from data simulated with one mouse annotation covered the true
abundance at close to their nominal level. Intervals from data simulated with
another were less accurate, many biased downward. Those authors attribute that
to the prior acting across a larger transcript set [@li2011rsem]. Uncertainty
is not spread evenly either: it is systematically larger for genes whose
isoforms resemble one another and for genes in large families of similar
sequence. So a transcript-level table has a different amount of doubt in every
row [@zhu2019swish].

That uncertainty can be carried into the differential test rather than
discarded at the boundary. Resampling reads to produce bootstrap replicates of
the abundance estimates lets a linear model separate the variance coming from
biological replication. It separates that from the variance coming from having
inferred the abundances in the first place
[@pimentel2017quantificationuncertainty].

Propagating it changes which transcripts are called. In a simulation with six
samples per group, the method consuming posterior samples held its false
discovery rate at the 1, 5 and 10 per cent targets. A rank-based method
ignoring quantification uncertainty tended to exceed the 5 and 10 per cent
targets for transcripts of medium-to-high uncertainty. From nine samples per
group upward a bootstrap-based competitor failed to hold the 5 and 10 per cent
targets. From fifteen upward it failed the 1 per cent target as well
[@zhu2019swish].

### The annotation bounds the question

A quantifier answers only the question its index allows. One widely used tool
estimates abundances for the transcripts it was handed, and cannot report
expression of a transcript absent from the annotation. So those authors say
that where many expressed forms are unannotated, successful application of
their workflow may require building out a more representative annotation first
[@love2018swimming].

The cost of incompleteness has been measured, and it depends on the organism.
Removing a fifth of the annotated transcripts from the index before quantifying
cost much more power to detect changed isoform usage in a simulated fly
transcriptome than in a simulated human one. Those authors restrict that
comparison to the counting methods combined with one differential test. They
offer isoform redundancy as a likely explanation. Human genes have enough
remaining isoforms to absorb the loss, while fly genes are often left with one
or none [@soneson2016prefiltering].

The sharper experiment deletes the dominant form. Removing the most highly
expressed isoform of every gene from the annotation leaves the reads of the
dominant form nowhere correct to go. That sharply degraded the accuracy of
every method except the two that refuse to assign ambiguous reads, which were
the least affected. One quantifier was in the most difficulty and a naive
read-proportioning scheme was the next most robust after those two
[@sarantopoulou2021comparative].

That same benchmark disagrees with the method papers. On simulated reads
carrying realistic artefacts the four model-based quantifiers did not perform
dramatically better than a naive scheme that splits ambiguous reads in
proportion to unambiguous ones. Even so, on idealised reads they were the most
accurate. Those authors read this as evidence that short reads are close to
exhausted as a source of isoform-level information
[@sarantopoulou2021comparative].

### Identifiability

Some abundances are not determined by the reads at all, and the share has been
counted. The design was 16 samples, and a swept assumption about how much of
expression the reference transcriptome accounts for, running from 10 to 100 per
cent. On that design, around 35 to 50 per cent of transcripts could carry
estimation error from non-uniqueness alone. For 20 to 47 per cent of all
transcripts the range of equally optimal values was wide enough that even the
rank of the transcript against its sibling isoforms was undetermined. About
half of these were not the transcripts made uncertain by finite sample size
[@zheng2022nonidentifiability]. Those figures are computed across a swept
parameter, not measured at one setting.

It is not only a theoretical worry. Of 257 differentially expressed transcripts
called at a false discovery rate of 0.01 in one dataset, 5 were flagged as
unreliable, as were 19 of 3,152 calls in another. The flag was raised because
the ranges of equally optimal abundance in the two conditions overlapped by
more than a quarter. Those overlaps are computed across the same swept
assumption, with the majority of calls robust where that share is above 40 per
cent [@zheng2022nonidentifiability].

Identifiability is a property of the library as much as of the gene. One
treatment puts it as a question about read length and fragment length
distribution, assuming a given transcriptome with coverage sufficient to
interrogate every junction. On those assumptions, the fragment length
maximising the number of identifiable human genes was about 400 to 600
nucleotides for coding genes, and 150 to 200 for long non-coding RNAs.
Combining two libraries of very different fragment lengths raised the
identifiable fraction further [@ferrerbonsoms2022fragmentlength].

It is also a property of the assay. Of 2,256 alternatively spliced human genes,
up to 97 per cent gave identifiable models from RNA-seq, a figure those authors
say was similar in mouse. That is against 69 per cent on the most comprehensive
splice junction array and 26 per cent on the human exon array, for which no
mouse figure is given [@hiller2009isoformdeconvolution].

### The methods disagree more than their error rates suggest

Four tools asked the same question of the same samples largely did not agree.
Of 7,116 cassette events all four measured and tested, each called between 133
and 274 significant. Of those, 370 were called by at least one and only 22 by
all four. Of 2,924 alternative splice site events, 352 were called by at least
one and two by all four [@trincado2018suppa2].

Low agreement is not explained away by false positives, which is the result
that makes it serious. Across ten methods on human long-read bulk data the
median pairwise overlap of the top ten ranked transcripts was between zero and
0.05. It reached only about 0.24 at the top five hundred. Median indices were
often below 0.1 in single-cell and spatial data. Nine of the ten methods had a
mean empirical false discovery rate below 5 per cent on the same datasets
[@zhang2026dtuframework]. The methods are each calibrated and they still
disagree about which transcripts matter.

Between laboratories the picture is worse: measured across 42 laboratories and
207 analysis pipelines on shared reference materials, isoform-level abundances
varied enough between laboratories that the laboratory effect often masked the
biological difference between samples. Restricted to the laboratories judged
high quality, mean correlation to the long-read reference was 0.71 and to
RT-qPCR 0.91 [@wang2026benchmarking].

An earlier multi-site, multi-platform study designed to measure reproducibility
found that relative expression could be reproduced across laboratories and
platforms once specific filters were applied. Of the features detected across
pairs of replicate sites, about 90 per cent of known genes but 87 per cent of
known exons and 83 per cent of known junctions were detected consistently.
Performance was worse at the transcript level than at the gene level, and
depended more strongly on which analysis pipeline was used
[@seqc2014assessment].

## Matching transcripts by intron chain {#sec-transcript-classes}

The intron chain is the comparison unit that makes transcript identity
checkable. Two transcripts match at intron-chain level when every intron has
identical coordinates and the counts agree. That implies all internal exons
match, but says nothing about where the transcript starts and ends. Terminal
boundaries are deliberately outside the definition [@pertea2020gffutilities].

The idea was in print by 2006. Comparing annotation tracks, one group treated
each model as an unbreakable chain of introns whose boundary coordinates on the
genome give the model a signature. It scored a pair of models by counting each
boundary plus one when the two share it, and minus one when it is unique to
either. Under that arrangement identical models always score best
[@thierrymieg2006aceview].

Four years later the same reduction became the matching rule of a comparison
tool. An assembled fragment counted as a complete match when some annotated
transcript had an identical chain of introns. Those authors state that rule
immediately after noting that because sequencing is stochastic the same
transcript assembled from two samples may come out at slightly different
lengths. They do not themselves say that the terminal boundaries are excluded
for that reason [@trapnell2010transcript]. The inference is natural and it is
the reader's, not theirs.

The long-read classification built on that unit has two known and two novel
categories, and the known ones are defined purely on junctions. A full splice
match reproduces every splice junction of some reference transcript, and an
incomplete splice match reproduces a consecutive run of them but not all. Neither
category says the ends agree, which is why an incomplete match can be a real
short isoform or a truncated cDNA [@tardaguila2018sqanti].

The novel categories are graded by how far a transcript departs from the
annotation's splice-site inventory. Novel in catalog uses only already-annotated
donors and acceptors, either recombined into new junction combinations or newly
paired with each other. Novel not in catalog introduces a donor or acceptor the
annotation does not contain [@tardaguila2018sqanti]. Every novelty count in this
book rests on that distinction, and @sec-catalogs is where it is taken apart.
## Splicing into decay {#sec-as-nmd}

The canonical rule for whether a stop codon is read as premature is positional. A
stop at least 50 nucleotides upstream of the last exon junction leaves an exon
junction complex downstream of it after the first round of translation, and that
complex is what triggers decay. The rule was established with reporter
constructs, not by survey [@lindeboom2016nmdrules].

Decay is not a property a transcript has but an event each translating ribosome
can trigger. Imaging single reporter messages in human cells showed cleavage
only after the first ribosome had reached the premature stop. The chance of
cleavage was the same at every subsequent round of translation, rather than
confined to a privileged first round [@hoek2019singlemolecule].

There are two exits from the pathway, an endonuclease cut by SMG6 and the
ordinary degradation route, and they are not alternatives. The second is the
cell's own degradation machinery, recruited directly: the SMG7 half of one pair
docks onto an enzymatic subunit inside the CCR4-NOT deadenylase. After that the
poly(A) tail is shortened, the cap removed and the body degraded. So a decay
target is handed to the same enzymes the cell uses on every other message
[@loh2013ccr4not]. Depleting SMG5 and SMG7 did not merely remove that route but
also switched off the endonuclease. That is because SMG6 cannot cut until SMG5
or SMG7 is present, and either one alone suffices. Those authors describe the
final step as requiring two things at once, phosphorylation of UPF1 and the
arrival of SMG5 or SMG7, rather than offering a choice of two routes
[@boehm2021smg5smg7].

The two branches are also redundant in what they act on. Knocking down UPF1,
SMG6 and SMG7 and rescuing each separately showed that SMG7 has a weaker effect
than SMG6. It reaches essentially the same genes, with only about 8 per cent of
expression change estimated as specific to one factor rather than the other
[@colombo2017nmdtargets].

### Deliberate decay

AS-NMD, also published as regulated unproductive splicing and translation, is the
proposal that cells splice deliberately into decay. An isoform is made in order
to be destroyed, so that the fraction of transcripts reaching protein is set
post-transcriptionally. On this reading an unproductive isoform is an output of
regulation rather than a failure of it [@garciamoreno2020asnmd].

The idea predates RNA sequencing: classifying reliably supported alternative
isoforms of known human genes found that a third of them contained premature
stop codons. Those authors proposed on that basis that coupling alternative
splicing to decay might be a pervasive way of setting protein output
[@lewis2003coupling].

A survey with decay inhibited put high-confidence targets at 2,793 isoforms
from 2,116 genes, expressed over two explicit denominators. Those are 19 per
cent of expressed protein-coding genes, and 22 per cent of the 9,440 genes
counted as alternatively spliced. Alternatively spliced here means producing
two or more expressed isoforms, including the decay targets themselves
[@french2020asnmdsurvey]. The second denominator contains the numerator, which
is worth noticing before the two figures are compared with anything.

The pathway's reach is not confined to protein-coding transcripts. Of the 1,000
highest-confidence targets in one cell line, identified with decay inhibited
genetically, 78 per cent coded for protein. In the same set, 9 per cent were
pseudogenes, 6 per cent long intergenic non-coding RNAs and 4 per cent
antisense transcripts [@colombo2017nmdtargets].

A catalogue built from decay-deficient cells rather than from annotation rules
runs to 302,889 assembled transcripts, a quarter absent from the reference. Of
those, 48,213 carry a premature stop by the 50-nucleotide rule, while 6,433 rose
significantly in three or more comparisons of decay-competent against
decay-deficient cells [@brittoborges2024nmdtxdb]. The gap between 48,213
predicted and 6,433 measured is the distance between a rule and an observation,
and no source read here resolves it.

### Whether it is regulation or noise

The claim that decay-coupled splicing is widespread regulation was contradicted
within three years. Profiling splice variants on microarrays across diverse
mammalian cells and tissues found that the stop-containing variants sat at
uniformly low levels wherever they were looked for. They did so whether or not
decay was acting, by means that abstract does not state. That led those authors
to suggest most reading-frame-breaking splicing is not under positive selection
and may carry no function [@pan2006evidenceagainst].

Where the non-productive products die bears on whether they are regulated at
all. Splicing intermediates were tracked across nascent, nuclear and mature RNA
in two human cell lines. That found transcripts using the weakest splice sites
3.3-fold more abundant in nascent than in nuclear RNA, against 1.1-fold for
canonical sites. Inhibiting translation-coupled decay chemically with
cycloheximide raised the transcripts using strong cryptic sites by 1.77-fold,
while leaving the weak-site ones at 1.1-fold. From that those authors argue
indirectly that the low-fidelity products are cleared in the nucleus, before
translation-coupled decay could reach them [@khokhar2026splicingnoise].

How decay was stopped changes the catalogue, which is why these surveys are hard
to stack. Of 47 genes whose messages were confirmed to rise when UPF1 was
depleted, only 17 also rose under cycloheximide, while 19 actually fell and 10
did not move [@mcglincy2010hnrnpa2b1]. Those three outcomes do not account for
every gene in the tested set. Genetic and chemical inhibition do not return the
same list, so a comparison between two surveys has to carry the method of each.

### Poison exons

Poison exons are not scattered curiosities but a family-wide arrangement. Each
of the human SR splicing regulators, with no exceptions among them, carries a
highly or ultraconserved element that is alternatively spliced. It is spliced
either as a cassette exon bearing an early in-frame stop or as an intron in the
3' untranslated region. In both cases the resulting message is destroyed rather
than translated, and mouse orthologues show the same patterns
[@lareau2007srgenes].

The autoregulatory loop runs in opposite directions for the two protein
families, and that polarity is what makes it homeostatic. Blocking decay in
mice and reading splicing-sensitive microarrays found a class of highly
conserved stop-containing exons whose inclusion makes the transcript
decay-sensitive. A separate genomic search identified more than 50 such exons.
The messages encoding splicing activators were sent to decay by an act of
splicing activation. Those encoding repressive proteins were sent to decay by
an act of splicing repression [@ni2007homeostatic].

Stated as mechanism, the two directions are one logic implemented twice. SR
proteins, which activate splicing, raise their own poison exon inclusion or
retain a 3' untranslated region intron when they are abundant. hnRNP proteins,
most of which act as splicing repressors, cause an exon to be skipped and the
frame broken when they are abundant. In both families a rise in the protein
sends a larger share of the gene's own precursor into decay. There are
documented exceptions, in which an hnRNP works the way an SR protein does
[@garciamoreno2020asnmd].

The hnRNP direction has a case measured at the protein level. Depleting UPF1
and reading protein changes by two-dimensional gel proteomics yielded 17
confirmed targets. That is a different 17 from the cycloheximide responders
above. Among them was a conserved event in the 3' untranslated region of one
hnRNP gene. Forcing that protein higher lowered the gene's own message,
while raising its decay-sensitive isoforms [@mcglincy2010hnrnpa2b1].

The conservation behind these exons is deep in one case and shallow in most.
Unproductive splicing of one SR gene is found in all animals examined and in
fungi, which makes it one of the few splicing events conserved between
kingdoms. Yet as the family duplicated, that ancient event was lost in the
paralogues and replaced repeatedly by new unproductive splicing. Ultraconserved
elements overlap the poison cassette exons of four of the eleven human SR genes
[@lareau2015splicingfactors].

Counted across the genome, frame-disrupting exons are numerous and only a small
subset is exceptionally conserved. 12,653 human exons were predicted from
annotation, with no decay inhibited and none of them measured, to send their
transcript to decay. Of those, 520 had high conservation at both splice sites
across 46 species. The highly conserved ones were enriched in genes encoding
RNA-binding proteins in a way that frame-preserving cassette exons were not
[@thomas2020poisonexons].

Forcing a poison exon out of its transcript costs cells growth, which is a
direct test rather than an inference from conservation. Paired guide RNAs
suppressed recognition of individual exons. In one cell line that depleted 43
per cent, or 169, of the targeted poison exons in expressed genes, against 58
per cent, or 170, of the upstream constitutive exons used as a comparison. In a
second line the figures were 13 per cent against 35 per cent
[@thomas2020poisonexons]. The poison exons matter less than the constitutive
ones and they do matter.

### A transcript can be routed to decay without a premature stop

Upstream open reading frames act on fate the way a premature stop does, and
whether they do depends on whether they are translated. Transcripts carrying
one were much more likely to peak in the single-ribosome fraction than
transcripts without. The figures are 31 per cent against 12 per cent when the
upstream start codon sat in a strong initiation context, and only 15 per cent
when it did not [@lloyd2020polysomefractionation].

In cells with UPF1 depleted, 14,348 transcripts whose stop codons were all in
the normal place nevertheless carried at least one upstream open reading frame.
Of those, 5,628 had a strong initiation context. Transcripts with a strong
upstream frame were about twice as likely to rise in abundance as transcripts
with none. Those authors read this as a second route into decay that does not
require the coding sequence to change [@french2020asnmdsurvey].

## Twelve bounds on the 50-nucleotide rule {#sec-nmd-limits}

The positional rule is the most quoted statement in this chapter and it is also
the most qualified. The qualifications are worth setting out together, because
each is a measurement and several come from one tumour cohort in which no decay
was inhibited anywhere in the design.

**It holds where it applies.** Across 9,769 human tumours with matched exome
and transcriptome data, stop codons in the last exon were followed by almost no
decay, while those further upstream were followed by a great deal. The
transition was abrupt at the 50-nucleotide boundary: efficiency of 1.7 per cent
in the last exon and 2.2 per cent within the final 50 nucleotides, against 84.7
per cent upstream [@lindeboom2016nmdrules].

**It applies to a small part of the sequence.** The same authors report the
rule as highly accurate wherever it applies, with near-complete escape for
every stop in that window. They note that the window covers only a small part
of a gene's sequence, and so is not pertinent for many of the stop codons that
actually occur [@lindeboom2016nmdrules]. A rule can be nearly always right and
still explain little.

**Applied across the genome it accounts for the smallest share of escapes.** A
decision-tree model trained on tumour efficiencies was applied to 120 million
predicted stop codons in 101,781 human transcripts. It put 55 per cent of all
possible stops as seen by decay. Escape was attributed to the last exon for 18
per cent of stops, to start proximity for 12 per cent, and to long exons for 12
per cent. It was attributed to the 50-nucleotide window for only 3 per cent. A
companion regression model, scored on a different threshold, instead split the
same stops into 51 per cent efficiently degraded, 22 per cent not degraded and
27 per cent in between [@lindeboom2019nmdetective]. Two models from one paper,
two partitions.

**It fails near the start codon.** In the same cohort, stops within 200
nucleotides of the start codon were followed by decay at 35 per cent
efficiency, against 93 per cent further along. Those in the first 100 coding
nucleotides were rarely degraded at all. Where an in-frame AUG lay downstream
of the stop, efficiency fell to 1.9 per cent against 57 per cent without one.
Those authors read this as translation re-initiation, while naming the distance
from the start codon to the stop, rather than the position of that AUG, as the
strong predictor [@lindeboom2016nmdrules].

**That start zone is far narrower when measured codon by codon.** In one gene,
with decay inhibited chemically by an SMG1 inhibitor, stops in the first 21
codons failed to trigger decay, with only a few showing weak activity. Activity
then rose to full strength across the next four codons. That transition is far
narrower than the 200-nucleotide zone inferred from tumour data
[@cortazar2025stopcodonscanning].

**The boundary itself is a gradient, not a boundary.** Every possible stop
codon was introduced along the second-to-last exon of one gene, with decay
inhibited by an SMG1 inhibitor and independently by cycloheximide. That gave a
smooth rise and fall of decay activity, peaking about 71 nucleotides upstream
of the last junction. There was measurable decay even at a codon inside the
window the rule predicts to be insensitive [@cortazar2025stopcodonscanning].
The 50-nucleotide line is a convention drawn across a curve.

**Long exons and distance to the normal stop are separate bounds.** In the same
cohort, a stop inside an exon longer than about 400 nucleotides was followed by
decay at 61 per cent efficiency, against 98 per cent elsewhere. Within those
long exons what mattered was how far the stop sat from the next junction
downstream. Separately, stops very far from where translation would normally
have ended were followed by less decay. That is 67 per cent efficiency in the
fifth of cases with the longest such distance, against 99 per cent otherwise
[@lindeboom2016nmdrules].

**Not every downstream junction counts.** Where a gene carries an intron inside
its 3' untranslated region, a stop in the second-to-last exon was followed by
almost no decay despite a junction lying downstream of it. That is 7 per cent
efficiency against 81 per cent for stops in exons further upstream. Those
authors read it as the decay-triggering complex being the one at the
second-to-last splice site [@lindeboom2016nmdrules].

**There is a route that needs no junction at all.** In human cells the distance
between a terminating ribosome and poly(A)-binding protein decided whether
termination counted as premature. So an ordinary stop codon could be made to
trigger decay by lengthening that distance. A premature one could be rescued by
folding the poly(A) tail or tethering that protein nearby [@eberle2008pabpc1].

**The long-3'-untranslated-region route does not appear to govern human decay
at scale, and this is disputed.** Across the tumour cohort, stops downstream of
the last junction or in intronless genes showed no relationship between decay
efficiency and how close the stop sat to the transcript's 3' end
[@lindeboom2016nmdrules]. A ribosome-load readout agrees: as 3' untranslated
region length increased, the share of transcripts peaking in the
single-ribosome fraction did not rise but drifted gently down. Three
transcripts whose long 3' untranslated regions trigger decay in reporter assays
were found carrying either an even spread of ribosomes or eight or more
[@lloyd2020polysomefractionation]. The opposite conclusion comes from a genetic
decay-inhibition catalogue in the same species. What that line gives is a
ranking of features by predictive value, rather than a measurement of what each
contributes. An intron inside the 3' untranslated region ranked first in a
high-confidence set of human targets, upstream open reading frames second, and
a long 3' untranslated region last of the three [@colombo2017nmdtargets]. So
the feature two analyses dismiss is one this analysis keeps, and keeps last.

**Escape is a subpopulation, not a property.** Identical molecules carrying the
same premature stop do not share one fate. In the single-molecule imaging
experiment, 5 to 10 per cent of the molecules of one reporter survived the
window in which the rest were cleaved, and then stayed largely resistant over
the window imaged. So a measured decay efficiency is an average over a
population containing a fraction that resisted for as long as it was watched
[@hoek2019singlemolecule].

**Steady-state abundance confounds decay with other effects.** In the same
codon-by-codon scan, 37 of 93 stop variants in one exon reduced splicing
efficiency by roughly a fifth to two fifths. Some variants stayed low even
after decay was inhibited. So the steady-state abundance of a stop-containing
isoform confounds decay with effects on transcription and splicing
[@cortazar2025stopcodonscanning].

Put together, the rules account for most but not all of what varies. A
regression on the tumour data explained 74 per cent of the variance in decay
efficiency, measured against the maximum observable variance given the noise in
the data. The canonical exon-junction model accounted on its own for nearly
half of the observed variance. Start-proximal escape accounted for 17 per cent
of what remained, and long exons for 4 per cent. Message half-life and distance
to the normal stop each took 1.6 per cent, and sequence motifs 0.1 per cent
[@lindeboom2016nmdrules].

One independent readout avoids inhibiting decay at all and agrees with the
junction rule. Human transcripts were sorted by how many ribosomes they
carried. The proportion whose peak abundance was in the single-ribosome
fraction rose sharply once the last junction lay 50 or more nucleotides
downstream of the stop. It rose from 15 per cent of transcripts without such a
stop to 35 per cent of those with one [@lloyd2020polysomefractionation].

## Nuclear retention is a fate of its own {#sec-nuclear-retention}

Being held in the nucleus is a fate in its own right, and it is where most
stably intron-retaining messages are. Separating nuclei from cytoplasm in mouse
cortical neurons after blocking transcription found 1,465 stable retained
introns in 922 genes out of 11,381 expressed genes. Of those 1,465
intron-retaining isoforms, 820, or 56 per cent, were at least twice as abundant
in the nucleus as in the cytoplasm. That is against 4 per cent of fully spliced
transcripts [@mazille2022intronretaining].

What separates a retained transcript from a decay target is that the retained
one can still be finished. Stimulating the same neurons sent intron-retaining
transcripts down two routes in the whole-cell measurement, with 83 after one
stimulus and 46 after another completing their splicing. 46 and 29 respectively
were instead destabilised, with their spliced counterpart unchanged
[@mazille2022intronretaining].

Low ribosome load is not proof of decay. Transcripts holding a retained intron
but no stop codon positioned to trigger decay were still over-represented among
messages carrying a single ribosome, at 22 per cent against 11 per cent for
cassette-exon transcripts in the same class. The two groups responded
indistinguishably to the genetic decay inhibition of the same laboratory's
UPF1-depletion dataset. Those authors judge decay unlikely to be what puts
retained-intron transcripts in the single-ribosome fraction and say another
mechanism is likely involved [@lloyd2020polysomefractionation].

### Detained introns

A separate name exists for the case where retention is the point. The term
detained intron was coined for an unspliced intron sitting in a polyadenylated
transcript whose other introns have already been removed. Its authors drew the
line against a retained intron explicitly. A retained intron is the product of
a splicing choice that leaves the sequence in a mature message exported to the
cytoplasm. A detained intron marks a transcript held in the nucleus until
splicing finishes or the molecule is destroyed [@boutz2015detainedintrons]. The
primary consequence is nuclear retention, after which the RNA either finishes
splicing and is exported or is turned over in the nucleus. Roughly 3,000 such
events were seen in mouse embryonic stem cells, and about a tenth changed when
the Clk kinases were inhibited [@jacob2017intronretention].

What makes them a kinetic class rather than a stable end product is a
half-life. After transcription was blocked, the detained introns assayed had a
mean half-life of 29 minutes, against 11 minutes for flanking introns. The two
were compared as two populations rather than intron by intron within a gene
[@boutz2015detainedintrons].

Detention responds to a signal in both directions, and only for part of the
pool. Two hours after mouse embryonic stem cells were given a Clk inhibitor,
325 detained introns in 295 genes changed in abundance, 137 falling and 188
rising. In the same experiment, 2,822 of the detained introns measured did not
change detectably [@boutz2015detainedintrons]. A regulated class with most of
its members unmoved is a reminder that a named mechanism need not act on
everything bearing its name.
## Isoforms per gene has three answers {#sec-scale}

The per-gene distribution of annotated isoforms is heavily skewed, and it differs
by biotype. Across all gene bodies in one annotation release the median is one
isoform. For protein-coding genes the median is six with a 75th percentile of
eleven, and only 14.6 per cent of protein-coding genes are left with a single
annotated transcript [@page2025annotations]. The typical gene body and the
typical protein-coding gene are not the same animal, which is why a per-gene
average needs its biotype attached.

Annotation and observation diverge sharply at the top of that distribution. The
same release lists 7,255 genes with ten or more isoforms, 256 with fifty or
more and 30 with a hundred or more. The same authors quantifying nine tissues
with long reads observed at most 105 isoforms for any gene body and 60 for any
protein-coding gene. That is accepting a single uniquely aligned read as
evidence [@page2025isoformdiversity].

The typical case is smaller again: expressed transcripts outnumbered genes by
an average factor of 1.12 in primary tissues, barely more than one transcript
for each gene [@gonzalezporta2013dominanttranscript].

Those three figures are not in conflict. One counts what annotation holds, one
counts what a deep assay detects, and one counts what is expressed at a level
worth calling expression. A chapter that quotes any of them without its rule has
said nothing. The rest of this book quotes all three, and @sec-catalogs takes up
what happens when a catalogue is treated as a count of biology.

## What this chapter commits the rest of the book to

Three habits follow from the material above, and the rest of the book keeps them.

A count without its rule is not a number. Isoforms per gene is six by
annotation, a hundred by deep detection and barely more than one by expression. And @sec-scale gives all three with their rules. The same holds for
retention prevalence, for poly(A) site counts, for microexon counts and for the
share of genes with several translated frames.

A measurement names its own bound more often than the field repeats it. The
positional rule for premature stop codons is reported by its own authors as
covering a small part of a gene's sequence. The splicing code's accuracy is
partly an accuracy on its own dataset. The positional rule for a regulator
rests on peaks that fall inside a responsive exon under 1 per cent of the time.
Each of those qualifications is in the source. And @sec-nmd-limits collects the
twelve for the decay rule in one place, because they are usually met one at a
time.

Independence has to be checked rather than assumed. Two sources agreeing is
worth something only if they are two sources. Several apparent agreements in
this chapter are one laboratory, one dataset or one classifier seen twice.
Where this book can establish only that two author lists share no name, it says
that rather than saying independent.

What survives of the functional claim, once those three are taken into account,
is the subject of @sec-how-functional. The catalogues that the counting rules
act on are taken apart in @sec-catalogs.
